title: Hevajra
reason: Khmer bronze sculpture of the tantric deity Hevajra dancing (Cleveland Museum of Art, 2011.143). The work is a multi-armed Buddhist icon erroneously filed under European medieval manuscripts; the minuscule tantric attribute inside one of sixteen skull cups does not constitute a genuine feline subject or visual motif.

original_record.title: Hevajra
original_record.title_original: Hevajra
original_record.culture: Northeastern Thailand, former kingdom of Angkor
original_record.description: Hevajra was an important figure signaling the practice of Buddhist rituals. King Jayavarman VII placed particular emphasis on Hevajra during consecration rituals and set up a colossal stone sculpture of dancing Hevajra at the east gate of his fortified city in the Khmer capital at Angkor. In the Cambodia of Jayavarman VII, tantric Buddhism became public and widespread, practiced together with other more mainstream forms of Buddhism, Hinduism, and ancestor worship. The iconography of Hevajra is described in detail in a text that bears his name, the Hevajra-tantra, first composed in India probably in the 800s. Hevajra has eight heads, sixteen arms, and four legs. His left hands hold images of Indic gods; wealth, death, sun, moon, fire, wind, water, and earth. In his right hands are animals: bull, lion, human, cat, camel, sheep, horse, and elephant. They all sit in skull cups, objects also used in tantric rituals. He dances on a corpse that embodies ignorance and is surrounded by eight yoginis who dance triumphantly in a ring around him. Yoginis functioned as intercessors between human practitioners and enlightened beings. Many bronze images of Hevajra were made during the reign of Jayavarman VII, but few survive in as pristine condition as this example. According to scientific analysis and curatorial reports, this sculpture survived in a clay vessel submerged in water, which accounts for its high tin content and unusual gray patina. Samples from the clay core reveal the presence of the mineral feldspar, a characteristic of clay from the Isaan plateau, on the other side of the mountain range not far from Banteay Chhmar, in present-day Thailand.
original_record.context: Cast in bronze in the Khmer Empire during the reign of Jayavarman VII (r. 1181–1218), likely in the Isaan region of present-day Thailand, for tantric Buddhist consecration rituals. Now in the Cleveland Museum of Art (inv. 2011.143).
original_record.feline_symbolism: The cat is one of eight animals cradled in skull cups in Hevajra's right hands, part of the tantric iconography prescribed by the Hevajra-tantra.
original_record.title_eng: Hevajra
original_record.submovement: Khmer bronze casting, Angkor period (reign of Jayavarman VII)

title: Lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel
reason: The Löwenmensch is a lion-man therianthrope (head of a cave lion), and lions and lion-men are excluded by the subject rule.

original.title: Lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel
original.medium: Carved mammoth ivory (Mammuthus primigenius)
original.description: Carved from a single mammoth tusk using flint stone scrapers, this upright zoomorphic statuette unites a bipedal human posture with the head of an extinct Eurasian cave lion (Panthera spelaea). The predator's muzzle, flattened forehead, and erect pinnae convey intense sensory vigilance, while seven incised parallel transverse notches mark the left upper arm. The polished surface finish was achieved through persistent abrasion using hematite powder and leather.
original.context: Discovered in August 1939 by Otto Völzing in the Stadel Cave within the Lone Valley of the Swabian Jura, the shattered ivory fragments were meticulously assembled over several decades following Joachim Hahn's 1969 reconstruction. Aurignacian hunter-gatherer communities dedicated an estimated four hundred hours of labor to craft this monumental spiritual effigy in the deepest recesses of the cave sanctuary.
original.feline_symbolism: Represents the earliest known manifestation of shamanic therianthropy, fusing human cognition with the apex predatory supremacy, nocturnal stealth, and physical ferocity of the cave lion.
original.title_eng: Lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel (Löwenmensch)

title: Panel of the Lions (Panneau des Lions)
reason: The Panel of the Lions at Chauvet shows cave lions hunting bison; lions, including cave lions, are excluded.

original.title: Panel of the Lions (Panneau des Lions)
original.medium: Charcoal and stump drawing with surface scraping on limestone cave wall
original.description: Executed in charcoal with stump shading on scraped limestone, a coordinated pride of sixteen cave lions stalks forward with lowered skulls, intense predatory gazes, and bunched shoulder musculature. The artist exploited the natural rock contours to impart volumetric swelling to the felines' flanks, omitting neck manes to accurately record the maneless anatomy of Pleistocene Panthera spelaea. Fine scrape marks around the feline contours produce pale outlines that detach the predators dramatically from the dark cave wall.
original.context: Discovered in December 1994 in the Ardèche valley, Chauvet Cave contains the earliest documented sanctuary of parietal art in Western Europe. Unlike Lascaux, where ungulates predominate, Chauvet is unique in dedicating over seventy percent of its iconography to dangerous apex carnivores situated in deep, acoustically resonant chambers.
original.feline_symbolism: Celebrates the collective hunting strategy, hierarchical coordination, and primeval stealth of the cave lion pride, serving as an Aurignacian locus of predatory veneration.
original.title_eng: Panel of the Lions (Chauvet Cave)

title: Neolithic Joint Burial of a Human and Wildcat
title_eng: Neolithic Joint Burial of a Human and Wildcat
reason: This is an archaeological burial of a real animal beside a human, not a work of art or object that depicts a cat; the subject rule purges entries about a living animal with no physical depiction behind them.

original.title: Neolithic Joint Burial of a Human and Wildcat
original.title_original: Sépulture néolithique d'un être humain et d'un chat
original.medium: Archaeological burial context; articulated feline and human skeletal remains (cast replica on display)
original.collection: Limassol Archaeological Museum, Cyprus (Cast of excavation at Parekklisia-Shillourokambos)
original.description: Excavated in close physical association, the articulated skeleton of an eight-month-old wildcat (Felis silvestris lybica) lies merely forty centimeters from the skull of an adult human. Both subjects were interred in symmetrical alignment within prepared sediment pits accompanied by polished greenstone adzes, marine seashells, and ochre deposits. The fully articulated state of the feline skeleton confirms intentional internment immediately following sacrifice, providing the earliest proven archaeological evidence of human-feline cohabitation.
original.context: Uncovered in 2004 by French archaeologist Jean Guilaine at Parekklisia-Shillourokambos in southern Cyprus, this burial predates Dynastic Egyptian feline records by more than four millennia. Because felids are not indigenous to Cyprus, the kitten was deliberately transported across the Mediterranean aboard primitive Neolithic seafaring craft from the Levantine mainland.
original.title_eng: Neolithic Joint Burial of a Human and Wildcat
original.dimensions: Grave pit approx. 80 × 60 cm; feline length approx. 45 cm
original.feline_symbolism: Documents the transition of the wild felid from opportunistic granary predator to venerated spiritual companion, deemed essential to accompany an elite human soul into the afterlife.
original.location: Limassol Archaeological Museum, Cyprus (Cast of excavation at Parekklisia-Shillourokambos)

original.title: Ivory Knife Handle of Gebel el-Arak
original.medium: Carved hippopotamus ivory handle with ripple-flaked chert blade
original.description: Carved in dense bas-relief from hippopotamus tusk, the handle depicts an iconic Master of Animals clad in Mesopotamian tunic holding two rampant lions in symmetrical heraldic restraint. Beneath the hero, hunting mastiffs and wildcats attack desert ibexes and gazelles, while the reverse illustrates hand-to-hand combat and Nilotic reed-bundle warships. Look closely at the upper register of the obverse handle to spot the two symmetrical lions rearing on their hind legs beneath the grip of the Master of Animals.
original.context: Acquired in Cairo in 1914 by the Louvre and reported to derive from Gebel el-Arak near Abydos, this ceremonial knife demonstrates direct Uruk-period iconographic influence entering Late Gerzean (Naqada IId) Egypt. The ripple-flaked flint blade represents the pinnacle of Neolithic lithic technology, married to Near Eastern dynastic visual vocabulary.
original.title_eng: Ivory Knife Handle of Gebel el-Arak
original.feline_symbolism: The restrained rampant lions embody chaotic wilderness tamed by divine kingship, an archetype foundational to emerging Pharaonic state ideology.

original.title_original: Cosmetic Spoon in the Shape of a Cat Holding a Fish (Eighteenth Dynasty, c. 1390 BCE)
original.description: Masterfully sculpted from dense hardwood, this cosmetic spoon represents an elongated swimming cat whose extended front paws clasp a hollowed tilapia fish forming the spoon's bowl. The feline's sleek body forms the handle, with incised ribbing detailing its spine and delicate black pigments highlighting its facial whiskers and claws. The fish's dorsal fin and scales are incised with geometric regularity, creating a functional lid slot for perfumed oils.
original.context: Dating to the reign of Amenhotep III, this luxury toilet implement reflects the sensual refinement of late Eighteenth Dynasty court culture. Used by aristocratic women to scoop scented salves and kohl cosmetics, zoomorphic spoons fused practical grooming with religious iconography.

original.title: Finger Ring with Recumbent Cat Bezel
original.description: Sculpted in full relief from vibrant reddish-orange carnelian, a miniature domestic cat curls serenely atop an integrated oval scaraboid bezel, its tail looped snugly against its flank. The feline's rounded ears, alert brow, and articulated spine are defined with microscopic lapidary cuts and high surface polish. The flat underside of the bezel is finely incised with protective wedjat eyes and solar papyrus emblems, swivel-mounted upon a gold wire hoop.
original.context: Ramesside period aristocrats favoured carnelian rings as protective finger talismans that served both ornamental and apotropaic purposes. Carnelian, associated with the blood of Isis and solar fire, was mined in Egypt's Eastern Desert under royal expeditionary supervision.
original.title_eng: Finger Ring with Recumbent Cat Bezel (Met 26.7.766)
original.medium: Carved translucent carnelian bezel with gold wire hoop
original.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
original.feline_symbolism: The fiery solar carnelian amplifies the cat's innate protective radiance, warding the wearer against venomous creatures while invoking the maternal blessing of Bastet.

title: Model Basket as Amulet
reason: Cleveland's own description says this Egyptian-blue amulet is a model basket associated with Bastet because her statuettes carry baskets of kittens; the amulet itself shows no cat.

original.title: Model Basket as Amulet
original.medium: Molded and pierced Egyptian blue (cuprorivaite)
original.collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
original.description: Molded from rich Egyptian blue (synthetic cuprorivaite), this miniature openwork basket simulates intricate woven reed construction with an arching handle and openwork sidewalls. Small perforated holes recreate woven textures, while an integrated suspension ring allowed the charm to hang securely from a necklace or linen mummy shroud. In Pharaonic iconography, such woven baskets were carried exclusively by statuettes of the cat-goddess Bastet to cradle litters of sacred kittens. Look closely at the openwork basket rim to observe the pierced reed-pattern perforations invoking the sacred kitten-carrying vessels of Bastet.
original.context: Gifted to the Cleveland Museum of Art by Dr. and Mrs. Jerald S. Brodkey in 1978, this miniature object exemplifies the high technological sophistication of Third Intermediate Period synthetic pigment manufacture. Egyptian blue was prized for its luminous turquoise brilliance, which did not degrade over millennia in tomb environments.
original.feline_symbolism: Directly evokes the domestic protection of Bastet, who was depicted bearing woven baskets of nursing kittens, serving as a talismanic emblem of maternal fecundity and childhood health.
original.title_eng: Model Basket as Amulet (Cleveland 1978.90)
original.submovement: Third Intermediate Period Lapidary & Vitreous Arts

original.title: Luristan Master of Animals Bronze with Confronted Felines
original.medium: Cast bronze with rich green patina (lost-wax process)
original.collection: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), Los Angeles, United States
original.description: Cast in lost-wax bronze with tubular finial architecture, a central heroic anthropomorphic figure firmly grips the throats of two rampant, confronted wild felines whose elongated bodies arch in symmetrical tension. The panthers or lions display gaping jaws with bared fangs, tubular protruding snouts, and sinuous curving tails that terminate in zoomorphic cockade terminals. The dynamic openwork composition balances predatory ferocity with stylized equestrian nomadic abstraction.
original.context: Produced by semi-nomadic metallurgists in the Zagros Mountains of western Iran during Iron Age II–III, Luristan bronzes were deposited as funerary finials and horse-trappings in stone cist graves. Their distinct hybrid iconography fused ancient Elamite, Mesopotamian, and indigenous mountain religious motifs.
original.feline_symbolism: Rampant felines embody untamed chthonic wilderness and dangerous mountain predators; grasping their throats asserts the shamanic hero's supremacy over mortal danger and chaotic predatory forces.
original.title_eng: Luristan Master of Animals Bronze with Confronted Felines (LACMA)

original.title: Marsh Scene with Cat and Birds
original.title_original: Marsh Scene with Cat and Birds
original.medium: Carved limestone in shallow low relief
original.collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, United States
original.description: Carved in refined bas-relief on fine white limestone, a slender swamp cat clambers up curving papyrus stalks in pursuit of nesting marsh fledglings, while a hoopoe bird and crane flutter in distress above. The animal's lithe musculature, outstretched claws, and predatory concentration are articulated with delicate low-relief modeling characteristic of Saite archaism. Look closely along the curving papyrus stems beneath the hoopoe bird to locate the agile cat scrambling upward toward the nesting fledglings.
original.context: Executed during the Twenty-Fifth to Twenty-Sixth Dynasty revival, this relief consciously replicates Old Kingdom wall compositions from the Saqqara mastabas while incorporating New Kingdom refinements. Purchased through the John L. Severance Fund in 1949, it demonstrates how Late Period sculptors turned to earlier classical dynastic models to restore national artistic purity.
original.feline_symbolism: The swamp cat hunting through papyrus marshes reenacts the cosmic subjugation of primordial wetland chaos, channeling solar vigor to safeguard eternal rebirth.
original.title_eng: Marsh Scene with Cat and Birds (Cleveland 1949.498)

title: The Striding Lion of Babylon (Processional Way of Ishtar)
title_eng: The Striding Lion of Babylon (Processional Way of Ishtar)
reason: The Processional Way panels show striding lions, the animal of Ishtar; lions are excluded by the subject rule.

original.title: The Striding Lion of Babylon (Processional Way of Ishtar)
original.medium: Molded and polychrome glazed baked brick relief
original.description: Constructed from individually molded baked bricks coated with vibrant vitreous glazes, a muscular lion strides majestically toward the left with gaping jaws, bared canines, and raised tail. The animal's leonine musculature, rippling mane, and sinewy shoulders are modeled in sculptural relief against a deep cobalt-blue glazed background. Ochre and white glazes delineate the fur texture, creating a luminous chromatic frieze that lined the ceremonial approach to the Ishtar Gate.
original.context: Commissioned by King Nebuchadnezzar II for the grand Processional Way connecting the Euphrates riverfront to the temple of Marduk in Babylon, this lion formed part of a sequence of 120 identical heraldic predators. German archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated the collapsed glazed brick fragments between 1899 and 1917, painstakingly reassembling them in Berlin.
original.feline_symbolism: Sacred beast of Ishtar, goddess of war, love, and imperial dominion, the striding lion projected invincible divine protection over the sacred capital while warning foreign visitors of imperial military supremacy.
original.title_eng: The Striding Lion of Babylon (Processional Way of Ishtar)

title: Ptolemaic Bronze Statuette of a Seated Cat
title_eng: Ptolemaic Bronze Statuette of a Seated Cat (Met 56.16.1, Frontal View)
reason: Duplicate: this is the same Met object 56.16.1 ('Cat Statuette intended to contain a mummified cat') already catalogued as met-bronze-cat-statuette-mummified-cat-332bce; only the photograph differs.

original.title: Ptolemaic Bronze Statuette of a Seated Cat
original.medium: Hollow-cast bronze with incised necklace
original.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, United States
original.description: Cast in hollow leaded bronze with remarkable sculptural authority, this large cat sits bolt upright with forelegs rigidly parallel and tail curled forward along the right plinth. The animal's triangular ears are pierced at the lobes for gold earrings, while an incised wadjet pectoral hangs from an engraved beaded necklace on its chest. The smooth, taut modeling of the shoulder blades and spine illustrates the refined Hellenistic influence infused into traditional Pharaonic votive casting.
original.context: Dedicated during the Ptolemaic Dynasty at a major Delta or Memphite sanctuary, this statuette was acquired by The Met in 1956 through the Harris Brisbane Dick Fund. The hollow interior was designed either to receive a mummified feline or to serve as a freestanding temple icon dedicated to Bastet.
original.title_eng: Ptolemaic Bronze Statuette of a Seated Cat (Met 56.16.1, Frontal View)
original.dimensions: Height: 26.5 cm; Width: 11.8 cm; Depth: 17.2 cm
original.feline_symbolism: Embodies the divine solar vigilance and maternal pacification of Bastet, acting as an eternal mediator between mortal supplicants and the cosmic pantheon.

title: Paracas Necrópolis Mantle with Flying Pampas Cats
title_eng: Paracas Necrópolis Mantle with Flying Pampas Cats
reason: The Commons photo shows a real Paracas Necropolis man's mantle at the Textile Museum (GWU), but its caption says nothing about felines, and I could not find any museum record for accession '91.388' or any source for 'flying pampas cats'; the cat content and the catalogue data cannot be confirmed.

original.title: Paracas Necrópolis Mantle with Flying Pampas Cats
original.title_original: Manto Paracas con motivos de felinos alados
original.medium: Embroidered camelid wool (alpaca and vicuña) on woven cotton ground
original.collection: The Textile Museum, George Washington University, Washington, D.C.
original.description: Monumental funerary mantle composed of a plain-weave cotton field framed by broad borders densely embroidered in stem stitch with supernatural pampas cats (Leopardus colocolo) in shamanic flight. Each feline figure is rendered in polychrome block-color style, displaying an arched spine, splayed clawed pads, and an elongated tail, while grasping severed trophy heads and chili pepper pods in its paws. Alternating color schemes of ochre, crimson, olive, and indigo animate the repeated motifs across the textile surface.
original.context: Excavated from the arid sand dunes of the Paracas Peninsula, this ceremonial mantle formed an exterior wrap for a mummy bundle belonging to a high-status elite priest or ruler. The hyper-dry desert climate preserved the saturated natural dyes derived from cochineal, indigo, and relbunium on fine camelid hair traded from the high Andes.
original.title_eng: Paracas Necrópolis Mantle with Flying Pampas Cats
original.feline_symbolism: Winged and soaring felines in Paracas Necrópolis iconography symbolize ecstatically transformed shamans traversing celestial realms, uniting predatory power with agricultural renewal.

title: Birth of the Virgin
reason: No source describes a cat in Carpaccio's Birth of the Virgin: Commons tags it only for rabbits, and Italian Wikipedia lists two rabbits at the open door and a woman preparing an animal for the kitchen, with no cat.

original.title: Birth of the Virgin
original.description: Painted for the Scuola degli Albanesi in Venice, Carpaccio’s narrative canvas recreates the Nativity of Mary inside an affluent patrician bedchamber. Soft Venetian light washes over timber-beamed ceilings and polychrome majolica tiles, where maidservants attend Saint Anne resting in her canopy bed. Look into the middle ground of the bedchamber near the wooden doorframe to find the small domestic cat crouched on the tiled floor, surveying the attendants tending to the newborn Virgin.
original.context: Carpaccio was celebrated for embedding sacred history within meticulously observed details of Venetian bourgeois domestic life. The presence of the house cat underscores the sanctity of the domestic threshold, transforming an everyday Venetian palazzo interior into sacred ground.
original.title_eng: Birth of the Virgin
original.medium: Tempera and oil on canvas
original.feline_symbolism: Symbol of domestic purity, peaceful domesticity, and the quiet sanctity of the Christian home.

title: Two Witches
title_eng: Two Witches with a Cat Familiar
reason: The Städel's own record of Baldung's Two Witches (1523) describes two nude witches, a Cupid, a bottle with a dragon-like creature and smoke, and its Iconclass tags list a he-goat but no cat.

original.title: Two Witches
original.medium: Oil on panel
original.description: In this nocturnal oil panel, Dürer’s foremost pupil depicts two nude sorceresses concocting a magical potion amidst billowing fumes and a stormy sky. Rendered with porcelain skin tones contrasting sharply against deep chiaroscuro shadows, the composition emphasizes supernatural menace and physical vulnerability. Look into the shadowed lower-left foreground to spot the crouching black cat staring directly outward with gleaming unblinking eyes, serving as the demonic familiar to the sorceresses.
original.context: Painted during the escalation of early modern witch trials in the Upper Rhine, Baldung’s witchcraft images popularized demonological theories found in the Malleus Maleficarum. The black cat was legally and theologically feared as a physical vessel of demonic agents assisting in illicit nocturnal rites.
original.title_eng: Two Witches with a Cat Familiar
original.feline_symbolism: Emblem of nocturnal sorcery, demonic espionage, and the uncanny agency ascribed to cats in early modern Europe.

title: Witchcraft (Stregoneria)
artist: Dosso Dossi (Giovanni di Niccolò de Luteri)
reason: No source mentions a cat in Dosso Dossi's Allegory of Hercules (Witchcraft) in the Uffizi; the detail photographs on Commons single out a small dog, a woodpecker and a magpie, but no cat.

original.title: Witchcraft (Stregoneria)
original.artist: Dosso Dossi (Giovanni di Niccolò de Luteri)
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: In this enigmatic courtly allegory from the Este court at Ferrara, Dosso Dossi weaves classical mythology with courtly satire and occult symbolism. Heavy impasto and saturated jewel tones of crimson and emerald illuminate a bizarre assembly gathered around a draped marble table. Look closely at the draped marble table in the lower-left foreground to detect the vigilant domestic cat perched beside an open manuscript, cocking its ears suspiciously toward the sorcerous assembly.
original.context: Court painter to Alfonso I and Ercole II d'Este, Dosso Dossi synthesized Venetian colorism with Ferrarese literary humanism, influenced by Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso. The alert cat embodies both auditory sensitivity in musical philosophy and mysterious intuition in hermetic lore.
original.title_eng: Witchcraft (Allegory of Hercules)
original.feline_symbolism: Symbol of acute sensory perception and occult discernment, capable of perceiving unseen spiritual forces.

title: Boy Pinched by a Crayfish with a Cat
title_eng: Boy Pinched by a Crayfish with a Cat
reason: No 'Boy Pinched by a Crayfish with a Cat' by Sofonisba exists: her crayfish subject survives as a drawing (Capodimonte) without a cat, and the image file is a Corsham Court group portrait 'Three Children with Dog'; the entry conflates these with Annibale Carracci's Two Children Teasing a Cat.

original.title: Boy Pinched by a Crayfish with a Cat
original.description: This pioneering Italian emotional study captures the instantaneous weeping reaction of a young boy whose finger is pinched by a freshwater crayfish held in a basket. Warm chiaroscuro washes across the child's tear-streaked face while a young companion chuckles in amusement. Look closely to the right of the weeping boy to spot the alarmed tabby cat recoiling with pinned ears and wide eyes at the child's sudden cry of pain.
original.context: Sofonisba Anguissola was praised by Michelangelo for her unprecedented ability to depict transient facial expression and spontaneous weeping from life. The inclusion of the reacting cat provides an empathetic biological mirror to human pain.
original.title_eng: Boy Pinched by a Crayfish with a Cat
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.feline_symbolism: An intuitive animal register of domestic distress, reflecting sudden shock and sympathetic physical alarm.

title: The Last Supper
reason: No source describes a cat in the San Trovaso Last Supper; the well-known Tintoretto cat (rummaging in a basket) belongs to his San Giorgio Maggiore Last Supper of 1592–94.

original.title: The Last Supper
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: Installed in the Blessed Sacrament Chapel of San Trovaso in Venice, Tintoretto’s horizontal canvas stages the Eucharistic mystery within a bustling nocturnal tavern. Vigorous diagonal perspectives, turbulent draperies, and flickering oil lamps impart dramatic kinetic momentum across the supper table. Look into the lower-right foreground beneath the serving bench to catch the opportunistic tabby cat climbing onto a wicker basket of bread rolls, greedily sniffing for scraps while Christ consecrates the bread.
original.context: Tintoretto deliberately contrasted the transcendent solemnity of Christ’s sacrifice with the earthy, distracting appetites of everyday Venetian life. The cat rifling through the bread basket grounds the divine narrative in mortal physical hunger.
original.title_eng: The Last Supper (San Trovaso)
original.feline_symbolism: Represents mundane, earthly appetite oblivious to the spiritual feast of the Eucharist taking place above.

title: Allegory of Vanity (Lady at Her Toilet)
title_eng: Allegory of Vanity (Lady at Her Toilet)
reason: No source I opened (Commons/Google Arts record of Toledo 1975.21, ECU Vanitas project, Eclectic Light essay) mentions a cat in Molenaer's 1633 Allegory of Vanity; one commentary notes the expected lapdog is replaced by a gilt statue, so the cat cannot be confirmed.

original.title: Allegory of Vanity (Lady at Her Toilet)
original.description: In this elaborate vanitas interior, a fashionable young Dutch woman sits before a dressing table laden with cosmetics, jewels, and musical instruments, absorbed in her worldly beauty. Molenaer employs crisp chiaroscuro and saturated hues, staging a dramatic moral confrontation between youthful luxury and inevitable mortality. Look closely at the lower-left foreground to spot the domestic cat playing with a skull resting on the floor, serving as a mordant memento mori counterpoint to the youthful vanity above.
original.context: Molenaer, husband of painter Judith Leyster, was a leading specialist in theatrical Haarlem moralities. The cat pawing at the human skull was an emblem of frivolous ignorance, warning that those consumed by worldly beauty are as unaware of death as a playing animal.
original.title_eng: Allegory of Vanity (Lady at Her Toilet)
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.feline_symbolism: Emblem of blissful ignorance and bodily playfulness confronting the sobering reality of mortality.

title: As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe
title_eng: As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe
reason: KMSKA's own text for inv. 677 (1638) lists the family, instruments and a single animal, a dog in the foreground eyeing the food; no cat is mentioned, and the Commons record of the 1638 Phoebus Foundation version mentions no animals.

original.title: As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe
original.title_original: Zo de ouden zongen, zo piepen de jongen
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.collection: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp
original.description: Jordaens orchestrates a boisterous Flemish family banquet overflowing with robust musical comedy, ruddy flesh tones, and energetic Rubensian vigor. Grandparents, parents, and children crowd around a laden table, singing lustily from sheet music while children blow recorders and bagpipes. Look towards the center-right of the boisterous gathering to find the sleek grey cat perched precariously atop the carved wooden armchair of the singing grandmother, gazing in bemusement at the pipe-playing youth.
original.context: Alongside Rubens and Van Dyck, Jordaens was the preeminent master of Antwerp Baroque art. The painting illustrates the Dutch proverb 'As the old sing, so pipe the young,' warning that children will inevitably imitate the vices, noisy follies, and indulgences of their elders.
original.title_eng: As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe
original.feline_symbolism: An amused, skeptical observer of human domestic bedlam, embodying quiet creaturely sanity amidst human folly.

title: Gōtoku-ji Temple Maneki-neko Votive Shrines
reason: Not a specific work: a temple and its ongoing votive custom of anonymous, modern mass-produced maneki-neko figurines; the 'c. 1650' date rests on legend, and Wikipedia records only that the temple, renamed Gōtoku-ji in 1659, is known as the 'cat temple'.

original.title: Gōtoku-ji Temple Maneki-neko Votive Shrines
original.title_original: 豪徳寺 招福猫児 (招き猫)
original.description: Hundreds of white ceramic Beckoning Cats (shōfuku nekoji) of graduated sizes stand densely massed upon open-air stepped wooden altars surrounding the temple's Shōfuku-den sanctuary. Each figurine is rendered with a raised right paw beckoning good fortune, a bright red collar with a golden bell, and black-spotted ears over a pristine porcelain glaze. Unlike commercial souvenir variants holding gold coins (koban), Gōtoku-ji's traditional temple cats hold no money, symbolizing spiritual opportunity rather than mere monetary greed.
original.context: According to temple history, Lord Ii Naotaka of Hikone domain took shelter beneath a tree outside the impoverished temple during a sudden thunderstorm in the early seventeenth century. Noticing the abbot's pet white cat Tama beckoning to him with raised paw from the temple gate, Naotaka approached the creature seconds before a lightning bolt destroyed the tree, inspiring him to designate Gōtoku-ji the official family burial temple of the Ii clan.
original.title_eng: Gōtoku-ji Temple Maneki-neko Votive Shrines
original.medium: White glazed terracotta and porcelain figurines with red and black enamel details
original.submovement: Edo to Contemporary Buddhist Temple Votive Craft
original.feline_symbolism: The maneki-neko embodies divine salvation, auspicious hospitality, gratitude, and the spiritual protection granted by loyal domestic animals.

title: A Young Girl at a Window with a Cat and a Mousetrap
title_eng: The Mousetrap (Girl at a Window Ledge)
reason: Could not confirm the work exists: no Dou 'Young Girl at a Window with a Cat and a Mousetrap' in the Leiden Collection; the linked image is the Musée Fabre kitchen scene with a woman and a boy with a mousetrap (836.4.14), whose record mentions no cat. The Leiden Collection's only Dou cat (GD-108, a separate entry in this batch) has a mousetrap only in its X-rayed underlayer.

original.title: A Young Girl at a Window with a Cat and a Mousetrap
original.title_original: Jonge vrouw in een venster met kat en muizenval
original.description: Gerrit Dou frames a smiling young maidservant inside an arched stone window niche (nisstuk), holding a wire mousetrap in one hand while cradling a tabby cat under her arm. Painted with microscopic fijnschilder precision using invisible brushstrokes, the surfaces render every texture: the cool stone masonry, reflective pewter pitcher, hanging dead fowl, and individual cat whiskers. The cat stares intently at the live mouse trapped behind the wire bars, its eyes dilated with predatory anticipation.
original.context: Rembrandt’s first and most famous pupil, Gerrit Dou founded the Leiden school of fijnschilders ('fine painters'). In Dutch genre painting, mousetraps symbolized love traps, domestic virtue, and the eradication of vice, with the cat serving as the active enforcer of domestic order.
original.title_eng: The Mousetrap (Girl at a Window Ledge)
original.medium: Oil on oak panel with arched top
original.feline_symbolism: Emblem of vigilance, domestic virtue, and the natural hunter deployed to eliminate domestic pestilence.

title: Myojakdo: Cats and Sparrows on an Old Tree (Full Hanging Scroll)
title_eng: Myojakdo: Cats and Sparrows on an Old Tree
reason: Duplicate: this entry describes Byeon Sang-byeok's Myojakdo (National Museum of Korea), which is already covered by byeon-sang-byeok-myojakdo-cats-and-sparrows-1750; its image (Joseon-Plum_Branch.jpg) is an unrelated 1888 plum painting by Yi Yu-won at the Met.

original.title: Myojakdo: Cats and Sparrows on an Old Tree (Full Hanging Scroll)
original.medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on silk
original.description: Byeon Sang-byeok paints an ancient zelkova tree where two cats engage in playful dynamic tension: one black-and-white feline scrambles vertically down the rough bark while another rests on the grassy ground, craning its neck upward. Six agitated sparrows flutter noisily among the upper leafy branches, counterbalancing the cats' concentrated movements. Layered micro-brush strokes build the thick tactile pelt of both felines with photographic precision upon sized silk.
original.context: A prominent member of the Joseon Royal Academy of Painting (Dohwaseo), Byeon Sang-byeok was so renowned for his hyper-realistic animal studies that contemporaries dubbed him 'Byeon Go-yang-i' (Byeon the Cat). His mastery of minute animalier brushwork was celebrated alongside his royal portraits of King Yeongjo.
original.title_eng: Myojakdo: Cats and Sparrows on an Old Tree
original.feline_symbolism: In Joseon iconography, the cat (myo) is a homophone for mao (耄, octogenarian longevity), while sparrows (jak) represent joyful tidings (jak, 鵲/爵), creating a courtly visual rebus wishing the recipient a joyous, healthy seventieth or eightieth birthday.

title: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Curled Sleeping Cat
title_eng: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Curled Sleeping Cat
reason: I could not confirm that a cat netsuke by Masanao of Kyoto exists at the British Museum: the entry's image is Masanao's goldfish netsuke (BM HG.421), and the Commons set of BM ivory netsuke lists Masanao's goldfish, rats and dog but no cat.

original.title: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Curled Sleeping Cat
original.title_original: 象牙彫 眠り猫根付 (京都正直)
original.description: Carved from polished marine ivory, this compact toggle represents a plump domestic cat curled tightly into a smooth organic sphere with its tail curving around its flanks. Masanao incises thousands of microscopic hair lines highlighted with dark ink pigment (*ke-bori*), capturing the tactile softness of the animal's coat. The cat's serene closed eyes and gently smiling muzzle project an aura of total domestic slumber designed to rest comfortably in the palm.
original.context: Masanao of Kyoto was widely celebrated as one of the preeminent animalier netsuke sculptors of the late eighteenth century, praised in the 1781 *Sōken Kishō* catalog for his lifelike tactile animal forms. Designed as functional toggles to suspend tobacco pouches or inrō medicine boxes from kimono sashes, netsuke demanded smooth contours devoid of snagging protrusions.
original.title_eng: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Curled Sleeping Cat
original.medium: Carved marine ivory with horn inlay eyes and incised ink stain
original.feline_symbolism: The curled sleeping cat embodies physical harmony, tactile pleasure, and tranquil protection against vermin and malevolent spirits.

title: Canton Painted Enamel Snuff Bottle with Cats and Peonies
title_eng: Canton Enamel Snuff Bottle with Cats and Peonies
reason: I could not confirm a Canton painted-enamel snuff bottle with cats at the Honolulu Museum of Art: the entry's image is a cloisonné bottle decorated with bats, and none of the 34 Honolulu snuff bottles on Commons mentions cats.

original.title: Canton Painted Enamel Snuff Bottle with Cats and Peonies
original.title_original: 廣東銅胎畫琺瑯耄耋富貴鼻煙壺
original.description: A miniature flattened oval copper snuff bottle decorated in brilliant polychrome Canton enamel depicting two playful cats among blooming tree peonies. Fine enamel brushwork renders the calico markings, alert rounded ears, and swishing tails of the cats as they chase butterflies across a pale turquoise ground. Gilded bronze mounts frame the miniature scenes, demonstrating the technical mastery of southern Chinese metalworkers.
original.context: Canton (Guangzhou) was the primary center for Chinese painted enamels on metal, blending European enamel techniques introduced by Jesuit missionaries with traditional Chinese auspicious iconography for Qing imperial and foreign markets.
original.title_eng: Canton Enamel Snuff Bottle with Cats and Peonies
original.medium: Painted polychrome enamel on copper, with gilded bronze stopper
original.submovement: Canton Workshop Enamel & Qing Court Decorative Arts
original.feline_symbolism: The pairing of cats (māo) with peonies (fugui) and butterflies (dié) forms the rebuses maodie and fugui, conferring blessings of immense wealth, noble status, and longevity past eighty.

title: Tamra Maew: Folio Depicting the Wichienmaat Cat
title_eng: Tamra Maew: Folio Depicting the Wichienmaat Cat
reason: The image is an unattributed photograph (author given as 'Cats of Thailand') of an unidentified Tamra Maew page; no manuscript, folio or holding institution can be confirmed, and the 'National Library of Thailand Nº 0543' record appears invented.

original.title: Tamra Maew: Folio Depicting the Wichienmaat Cat
original.title_original: ตำราแมว: แมววิเชียรมาศ
original.description: Rendered with pale fawn pigment and deep chocolate-brown points upon traditional khoi paper, this manuscript folio depicts the Wichienmaat (literally 'Moon Diamond' or Seal Point Siamese) seated in regal profile. The feline features distinctive almond-shaped blue eyes, dark ears, paws, and tail tip, delineated by delicate black ink contours alongside celebratory Thai poetic verse. Monastic illustrators carefully recorded these anatomical color markers to differentiate sacred breeds maintained within royal and religious compounds.
original.context: The Wichienmaat is revered in Thai history as the aristocratic progenitor of the modern Siamese cat, historically reserved for royalty and high-ranking Buddhist abbots in the ancient capitals of Ayutthaya and Bangkok. These cats roamed the gilded cloisters of Buddhist wats, where their keen vigilance protected fragile palm-leaf Tripitaka canons against vermin.
original.title_eng: Tamra Maew: Folio Depicting the Wichienmaat Cat
original.medium: Folding manuscript leaf (samut khoi); opaque watercolor and ink on mulberry paper
original.dimensions: Folding book format (c. 11 × 34 cm per folio)
original.submovement: Ayutthaya to Early Rattanakosin Manuscript Illumination
original.feline_symbolism: The Wichienmaat cat signifies radiant celestial light, prosperity, and spiritual fortune, believed to bring divine blessings to any household or monastery where it resided.

title: Neko-jinja: The Cat Shrine of Tashirojima
title_eng: Neko-jinja: The Cat Shrine of Tashirojima
reason: Entry is a place (a shrine on Tashirojima island), not a specific work; its image is a 2024 tourist photograph tagged 'Cat island' by Flickr user Maarten Heerlien, and the dimensions and inventory number are invented.

original.title: Neko-jinja: The Cat Shrine of Tashirojima
original.title_original: 田代島 猫神社 (美止利神社)
original.description: Nestled in the cedar woods of Tashirojima island, this rustic Shinto shrine features a small wooden sanctuary building fronted by a carved stone torii gate and numerous stone cat statues and votive figurines. Fishermen and visitors deposit canned cat food, ceramic feline figurines, and engraved wooden plaques (*ema*) to honor the spirits of deceased island cats. The shrine grounds serve as a living sanctuary where dozens of free-roaming domestic felines congregate in peaceful coexistence.
original.context: Historically, the islanders of Tashirojima raised silkworms and depended on domestic cats to protect the cocoons from mice; later, local fishermen observed cat behavior to predict weather and sea conditions. When an island fisherman accidentally injured a cat while harvesting rock ballast in the late Edo period, he buried the creature with great remorse and established Neko-jinja to pacify its spirit and pray for bountiful catches.
original.title_eng: Neko-jinja: The Cat Shrine of Tashirojima
original.medium: Carved stone shrine sanctuary, torii gate, and feline votive offerings
original.submovement: Tōhoku Shinto Folk Veneration Architecture & Sculpture
original.feline_symbolism: The deified feline (*neko-gami*) represents maritime safety, bountiful fishing hauls, and deep spiritual reciprocity between humans and working animals.

title: Young Tiger Playing with Its Mother (Jeune tigre jouant avec sa mère)
title_eng: Young Tiger Playing with Its Mother
reason: The work catalogued is Delacroix's Louvre painting Étude de deux tigres, dit aussi Jeune tigre jouant avec sa mère (Salon of 1831), which shows only tigers; tigers are excluded by the subject rule, and the 'studies of cats' in the id does not match the work described.

original.title: Young Tiger Playing with Its Mother (Jeune tigre jouant avec sa mère)
original.title_original: Jeune tigre jouant avec sa mère, dit aussi Étude de deux tigres
original.description: In a mountainous wilderness under stormy skies, a recumbent tigress watches over her playful cub as it rolls playfully onto its back with claws extended and teeth bared. Delacroix deploys sweeping, energetic brushstrokes and vibrant broken color, contrasting the supple musculature and tawny pelt of the adult with the agile, tumbling form of the juvenile. A passionate observer of big cats at the Jardin des Plantes menagerie alongside sculptor Antoine-Louis Barye, Delacroix famously remarked that tigers were merely enormous domestic cats infused with primordial electrical force.
original.context: Exhibited at the Salon of 1831, this monumental painting embodies the Romantic fascination with untamed sublime nature and maternal instinct among apex predators. Acquired by the Louvre in 1980, it remains one of Delacroix's crowning animalier compositions.
original.title_eng: Young Tiger Playing with Its Mother
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.feline_symbolism: Delacroix elevates the felid into the supreme embodiment of fierce passion, untamed nature, and the sublime harmony between lethal violence and maternal affection.

title: Hokusai Manga: Vol. 11 (Sketches of Cats and Small Animals)
reason: The cited page (BnF Gallica btv1b72003895, image 69 of 77, Hokusai Manga vol. 11) exists, but neither its BnF/Commons metadata (subjects: landscapes, animals, plants) nor any page opened confirms that this spread shows cats, so the cat subject could not be confirmed.

original.title: Hokusai Manga: Vol. 11 (Sketches of Cats and Small Animals)
original.title_original: 北斎漫画 十一篇 (猫の写生)
original.description: Across the double-page spread of his famous sketchbook manual, Hokusai captures the multifaceted gestures of domestic cats through spontaneous, calligraphic woodcut lines and subtle grey and flesh-pink washes. Felines are shown in varied attitudes: curled in deep sleep, arching spines during a morning stretch, crouching to stalk prey, and curiously investigating insects. The artist's energetic brush economy isolates the anatomical essence of feline motion with effortless vitality.
original.context: Published across fifteen volumes between 1814 and 1878, the *Hokusai Manga* served both as an instructional model book for aspiring painters and an encyclopedic visual digest of Japanese life, folklore, and natural history for the public. Hokusai insisted on obsessive empirical observation (*shasei*), filling hundreds of sketchbooks with animal gestures studied directly from nature.
original.title_eng: Hokusai Manga: Vol. 11
original.medium: Woodblock-printed book illustration; ink and light pink/grey wash on paper
original.submovement: Late Edo Manga & Life Sketch Woodblock Printmaking
original.feline_symbolism: The sketches celebrate the unconstrained physical agility, fluid grace, and kinetic vitality of cats as living exemplars of natural design.

original.medium: Woodblock print detail; ink and color on paper
original.description: This close study focuses on a curled tortoiseshell cat grooming its hind leg while its companion naps contentedly with curled paws and closed eyes. Kuniyoshi captures the velvety texture of feline fur through graduated ink shading and microscopic carved lines defining each contour. The naturalistic observation of a cat's idiosyncratic flexibility reveals an artist who sketched his pets continuously throughout the working day.
original.context: Kuniyoshi kept an album of quick life sketches (shasei) devoted entirely to feline gestures, which he consulted when composing complex multi-figure prints. His studio apprentices were required to sketch the household cats in various poses as a core exercise in life drawing.
original.title_eng: Cats in Different Poses (Detail)
original.title_original: 猫の当字 (細部: 眠りと毛づくろい)
original.submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)

original.title: Cat Under Mosquito Netting (Detail from Edo Bijin-ga)

original.submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
original.medium: Woodblock print detail; ink and color on paper
original.description: An inquisitive calico cat peers with wide amber eyes from beneath the hem of a draped green summer mosquito net (kaya), pawing gently at the woven border. Kuniyoshi renders the fine white and tortoiseshell markings of the feline's coat with delicate gouged woodblock lines, contrasting the animal's solid form against the sheer gauzy weave of the netting. The arched spine and poised forepaw capture the silent stealth of a house cat exploring domestic interiors.
original.context: Edo bijin-ga (pictures of beautiful women) frequently paired refined courtesans or townswomen with lively domestic pets to introduce psychological depth and sensual intimacy. Kuniyoshi observed that domestic cats were fascinated by gauze mosquito nets, turning routine household furniture into arenas for feline curiosity.
original.title_eng: Cat Under Mosquito Netting
original.feline_symbolism: The inquisitive house cat represents domestic contentment, summertime leisure, and the playful charm of Edo everyday life.

original.title: Cat Pouncing on Bonito Flake (Detail Study)
original.title_original: 鰹節を捕らえる猫 (細部)
original.submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
original.medium: Woodblock print detail; ink and color on paper
original.description: This intimate detail captures a calico cat in the thrilling instant of seizing a dried bonito flake, pinning the morsel against the floor with razor-sharp unsheathed claws. The feline's ears are pulled back in intense concentration, its whiskers fan outward, and its coiled tail demonstrates kinetic potential. Kuniyoshi's sensitive woodblock cutting delineates the dense soft fur along the flank and the taut tension of the feline shoulder muscles.
original.context: Japanese domestic cats were historically fed rice mixed with dried bonito shavings (katsuobushi), creating an inseparable association between cats and the fishmonger's trade. Kuniyoshi's keen observational eye elevated these spontaneous micro-dramas of domestic pet behavior into celebrated touchstones of animalier art.
original.title_eng: Cat Pouncing on Bonito Flake
original.feline_symbolism: The pouncing cat personifies predatory joy, intense sensory focus, and the uncomplicated delights of domestic animal life.

title: Station 38: Fujikawa (Buchi-kowa) from the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō

original.title: Station 38: Fujikawa (Buchi-kowa) from the Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō
original.title_original: 藤川 (ぶちこわ) - 猫飼好五十三疋
original.submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
original.medium: Woodblock print sheet (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
original.collection: British Museum / Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
original.description: In this celebrated section from the Fifty-Three Stations triptych, Kuniyoshi renders a spotted tortoiseshell cat arching its back and hissing with flattened ears as it faces a competitor. The station name 'Fujikawa' is transformed through phonetic punning into buchi-kowa (meaning 'a spotted cat is frightening'), visualised through the feline's ferocious defensive grimace and raised fur. Precise woodblock registration highlights the calico patches and sharp white claws gripping the floor.
original.context: Kuniyoshi's linguistic puns delighted Edo townsfolk who took pride in solving visual charades (mitate-e). His uncanny understanding of cat psychology allowed him to depict genuine territorial disputes and defensive displays with unflinching anatomical veracity.
original.title_eng: Station 38: Fujikawa (Buchi-kowa)
original.feline_symbolism: The bristling tortoiseshell cat represents territorial tenacity, comedic bluster, and the expressive emotional repertoire of domestic felids.

original.title: Tamra Maew: Folio Depicting the Auspicious Suphalak Cat
original.title_original: ตำราแมว: แมวศุภลักษณ์
original.artist: Anonymous Thai Court Scribe and Painter
original.description: Rendered in traditional Thai manuscript style, this folding samut khoi leaf illustrates the reddish-copper Suphalak cat seated in profile with arched neck, golden eyes, and dark-toned extremities. Precise black ink outlines define the feline's slender muscular contours, accompanied above by poetic Thai khlong stanzas inscribing its auspicious physical traits. Painted with mineral pigments upon treated mulberry bark paper, the composition exemplifies royal zoological treatises cataloging native felids.
original.context: Originating in the Ayutthaya Kingdom and recopied into the Rattanakosin period, the Tamra Maew treatises recorded seventeen auspicious cat breeds believed to bring prosperity, longevity, and royal protection to their owners. Monks and royal courtiers preserved these manuscripts in temple and palace libraries, venerating cats as spiritual companions and diligent protectors of sacred Buddhist palm-leaf scriptures from insect infestation.
original.title_eng: Tamra Maew: Folio Depicting the Auspicious Suphalak Cat
original.medium: Folding manuscript leaf (samut khoi); ink and mineral color on mulberry paper
original.dimensions: Folding book format (c. 11 × 34 cm per folio)
original.feline_symbolism: In Thai cosmological belief, the Suphalak cat embodies royal favor, health, and prosperity, serving as a talismanic ward against malevolent spirits and misfortune.

title: Minhwa Hojakdo: Magpie and Leopard-Cat Under Pine Tree
title_eng: Minhwa Hojakdo: Magpie and Leopard-Cat Under Pine Tree
reason: The only matching Honolulu Museum of Art work is 'Tiger and Magpies (hojakdo)', 19th-century Joseon, acc. 9502.1, which the museum calls a tiger, and the entry's source_url is an unrelated NGA drawing of Pennsylvania folk art.

original.title: Minhwa Hojakdo: Magpie and Leopard-Cat Under Pine Tree
original.medium: Hanging scroll; ink and mineral colors on mulberry paper (hanji)
original.description: Executed in bold, expressive folk style, this hanging scroll depicts an animated leopard-cat seated beneath a stylized pine tree, grimacing with bulging circular eyes, bared fangs, and whiskered cheeks. The animal's mottled pelt combines decorative tiger stripes and leopard rosettes rendered in black ink and ochre pigments over fibrous mulberry paper. Perched safely in the upper boughs, an iridescent green-and-black magpie squawks downward, teasing the grounded feline.
original.context: Minhwa folk paintings were produced by itinerant craftsmen for commoner households to celebrate the New Year (sehwa). These paintings decorated entry gates and inner rooms during the Lunar New Year, serving both as apotropaic charms and humorous satirical allegories during the late Joseon period.
original.title_eng: Minhwa Hojakdo: Magpie and Leopard-Cat Under Pine Tree
original.feline_symbolism: The wild feline (ho/beom) functions as an apotropaic guardian warding off evil spirits and disease (byeoksa), while the mocking magpie symbolizes good tidings, subtly satirizing corrupt magistrates outwitted by the common folk.

title: Imado Ware Marushime-neko Terracotta Figurine
reason: The only source is a Commons photo uploaded as 'own work' by the user Marusime, captioned 'Imado-yaki Marushime-neko, Kaei-Ansei style (風型)', i.e. a figure in the style of the 1850s with no maker, date or collection; no Edo-Tokyo Museum record or inventory number could be found.

original.title: Imado Ware Marushime-neko Terracotta Figurine
original.title_original: 今戸焼 丸〆猫 (嘉永安政風型)
original.description: Modeled from coarse Asakusa alluvial clay and painted with chalky white slip, this seated folk cat raises its left paw in a beckoning gesture while bearing the auspicious circled *shime* mark on its haunch. Painted black spots adorn its back and ears, while a dab of red mineral pigment highlights its collar, inner ears, and nose. The simple, charming modeling of the clay reflects the unpretentious folk charm of traditional Edo terracotta toys.
original.context: Produced by roof tile and pottery kilns in Imado near Asakusa Shrine, the *Marushime-neko* is recognized by cultural historians as the earliest documented historical prototype of the modern *maneki-neko*. According to late Edo records, an impoverished elderly woman in Asakusa was forced to abandon her beloved pet cat, who subsequently appeared in a dream advising her to mold its likeness in clay; the resulting figurines sold out immediately at the gates of Sensō-ji Temple, rescuing her from destitution.
original.title_eng: Imado Ware Marushime-neko Terracotta Figurine
original.medium: Low-fired painted terracotta (e-tsuchiningyō) with white slip, black sumi, and red pigment
original.submovement: Late Edo Folk Clay Figurine Craft (Imado-yaki)
original.feline_symbolism: The circled *shime* crest (丸〆) signifies 'wealth and good luck gathered round without leaking away', embodying feline benevolence, good luck, and economic salvation.

title: Crimean Tom (Sevastopol Tom)
reason: The entry is a biography of a real cat; the cited National Army Museum record (1958-02-40-1) returns 404, no albumen photograph of Tom is documented, and the stuffed cat the NAM received in 1958 is, per the museum, not proven to be Tom.

original.title: Crimean Tom (Sevastopol Tom)
original.description: An early military photograph recording Crimean Tom, the celebrated tabby cat discovered by Lieutenant William Gair among the bombed rubble of Sevastopol during the Crimean War in 1855. Mounted alertly upon a display base, the striped domestic feline possesses a dense coat, alert posture, and calm gaze that endeared him to British soldiers whom he guided to concealed Russian provisions. Following his death in England, Tom's pelt was preserved and acquired by the Royal United Services Institute, remaining one of the Victorian era's most storied animal military mascots.
original.context: During the brutal Siege of Sevastopol, British and French forces faced starvation until Lieutenant Gair observed this stray cat repeatedly emerging unbothered from cellar ruins; following him revealed subterranean grain caches and cellar stores that saved numerous garrison troops.
original.title_eng: Crimean Tom (Sevastopol Tom)
original.medium: Albumen silver print photograph
original.feline_symbolism: The historic wartime mascot representing feline resilience, lifesaving providence, and cross-species camaraderie amidst industrial siege warfare.

title: The Mummified Cat and Rat of Christ Church Cathedral ('Tom and Jerry')
title_eng: The Mummified Cat and Rat of Christ Church Cathedral ('Tom and Jerry')
reason: The 'Cat and the Rat' in the crypt of Christ Church Cathedral, Dublin are naturally desiccated animal remains in a display case, not a work of human culture; the entry's 'Natural desiccation' artist line says as much, and its medieval/ecclesiastical taxonomy for a c. 1850s find is wrong.

original.title: The Mummified Cat and Rat of Christ Church Cathedral ('Tom and Jerry')
original.title_original: The Mummified Cat and Rat of Christ Church Cathedral
original.description: Pair of naturally mummified specimens comprising a domestic cat and a large rat, discovered frozen in eternal pursuit within the pipework of the cathedral organ. Desiccated by the dry drafts of the organ casing, the cat's skeletal form remains fully covered in taut parchment-like skin, showing outstretched limbs, flexed claws, and an open jaw reaching toward the fleeing rodent. Displayed together horizontally within a glass case, the specimens form a dramatic tableau of predator and prey halted mid-stride.
original.context: Discovered during routine organ cleaning in the 1860s at Christ Church Cathedral in Dublin, the cat and rat were preserved when the cat became trapped behind the organ woodwork while chasing the rat. The famous discovery entered local folklore and Dublin literary history, famously referenced by James Joyce in Finnegans Wake as 'as cat and rat in the organ of Christ Church'.
original.title_eng: The Mummified Cat and Rat of Christ Church Cathedral ('Tom and Jerry')
original.medium: Naturally desiccated mummified domestic cat and rat specimens mounted in exhibition vitrine
original.collection: Christ Church Cathedral Crypt, Dublin, Ireland
original.feline_symbolism: Representing the eternal cycle of pursuit in Irish folk imagination, 'Tom and Jerry' serves as enduring physical evidence of the historic role of church mousers protecting cathedral organ bellows, leather valves, and choir vestments from rodent destruction.
original.location: Christ Church Cathedral Crypt, Dublin, Ireland

title: Matagot / Chat d’Argent (The Money Cat)
reason: The matagot is a folklore idea; the source_url is the Wikipedia article on the legend, and no specific woodcut in the Mucem (or anywhere) matching 'Matagot / Chat d'Argent, 28 x 20 cm, Nº 0658' could be identified.

original.title: Matagot / Chat d’Argent (The Money Cat)
original.description: A traditional popular print depicting the Matagot (or Chat d'Argent), the mythical feline of Gascon and Provençal folklore believed to inhabit crossroads and rustic farmsteads. Delineated in bold, expressive woodcut contours with hand-inked crosshatching, the enigmatic black cat is rendered with luminous, piercing pupils and an arched, bushy tail, guarding a cache of silver coins. Folk superstition dictated that whoever captures and hospitably shelters a Matagot will receive a fresh gold coin each morning at dawn.
original.context: Deeply rooted in rural southern French occult traditions and collected in nineteenth-century folklore anthologies by Paul Sébillot, the Matagot fused older pagan beliefs in household spirit guardians with medieval superstitions regarding witches' feline familiars.
original.title_eng: Matagot / Chat d’Argent (The Money Cat)
original.medium: Woodcut and typography on paper
original.collection: Musée des Civilisations de l’Europe et de la Méditerranée, Marseille
original.feline_symbolism: Personification of prosperity, magical retribution, and the capricious rewards granted to humans who honor domestic spirit beasts.

title: Sleeping Cat (Le Chat dormant)
reason: Existence cannot be confirmed: the only sources are a WikiArt page (no references, 'Private Collection', edited 2011) and the Commons file copied from it; no catalogue raisonné, museum or sale record was found, and the entry's 'Private Collection, Paris', 50 x 60 cm and inventory number are unsupported.

original.title: Sleeping Cat (Le Chat dormant)
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: A striped tabby cat sleeps peacefully curled upon the yellow woven rush seat of a rustic wooden chair, framed by a dark, earthy background. Painted when Renoir was twenty-one years old while studying in Charles Gleyre's Paris studio alongside Monet and Sisley, the canvas relies on rich, tactile impasto and subtle tonal transitions rather than broken Impressionist color. Renoir models the soft weight and velvety texture of the sleeping animal with affectionate, naturalistic brushwork.
original.context: Painted in 1862 at the very outset of Renoir's artistic career, this rare early canvas reveals his initial allegiance to Courbet's Realism and Chardin's still lifes. It marks the inception of Renoir's lifelong curatorial love affair with feline subjects.
original.title_eng: Sleeping Cat
original.feline_symbolism: The sleeping cat symbolizes peaceful domestic shelter, warmth, and the quiet dignity of everyday rustic life.

title: Torikeshitai: Courtesan Usugumo of the Miuraya with Her Pet Cat
title_eng: Torikeshitai: Courtesan Usugumo with Her Pet Cat

original.title: Torikeshitai: Courtesan Usugumo of the Miuraya with Her Pet Cat
original.title_original: 見立多以尽 取消したい (三浦屋薄雲)
original.description: The celebrated top-ranking courtesan Usugumo Dayū stands in her private quarters draped in an elaborate tortoiseshell comb headdress and luxurious trailing kimonos, holding a crumpled letter in emotional distress. At her bare feet, her beloved white house cat rubs affectionately against her scarlet undergarment, purring with arched spine and upright tail in total sympathy. Yoshitoshi's refined woodblock cutting captures the cat's silky white fur and the delicate emotional solace it offers its troubled mistress. Look closely at the lower right corner beneath the folds of the courtesan's scarlet under-robe to find her white pet cat rubbing affectionately against her feet.
original.context: Usugumo Dayū of the Miuraya brothel in Yoshiwara was legendary in Edo folklore for her obsessive love for her cat, carrying it everywhere in a silk bag and feeding it silver dishes. When an overzealous samurai suspected the cat of being a shapeshifting demon and severed its head, the flying head intercepted a poisonous viper poised to strike Usugumo in the rafters, revealing the feline's supreme devotion and prompting the creation of the first wooden maneki-neko in her honor.
original.title_eng: Torikeshitai: Courtesan Usugumo with Her Pet Cat
original.medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
original.feline_symbolism: The affectionate cat embodies unconditional loyalty, emotional solace, and self-sacrificing devotion to its beloved human protector.

title: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Sleeping Cat
title_eng: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Sleeping Cat

original.title: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Sleeping Cat
original.title_original: 象牙彫 眠り猫根付 (直斎)
original.medium: Carved marine ivory with horn inlay eyes and dark pigment stain
original.collection: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
original.description: Carved from dense cream-toned marine ivory, this tactile netsuke depicts a sleek domestic cat curled in blissful repose with its tail wrapped neatly around its hindquarters. The sculptor incises fine rhythmic fur lines across the flank, highlighting individual hairs with subtle sepia washes, and embeds polished dark horn for the closed eyes. The rounded, seamless contours create an ideal tactile form designed to glide effortlessly through the fingers of its owner.
original.context: During the Meiji transition, when Western clothing began replacing traditional kimonos, master netsuke carvers pivoted toward producing hyper-refined miniature sculptures for discerning European and American collectors. Chokusai continued the celebrated naturalistic animalier traditions established by Kaigyokusai Masatsugu, emphasizing quiet domestic serenity.
original.feline_symbolism: The sleeping cat symbolizes peaceful household contentment, tactile comfort, and the tranquil harmony of domestic sanctuary.
original.title_eng: Carved Ivory Netsuke of a Sleeping Cat

title: Young Girl with a Cat (Jeune fille au chat)
reason: The only trace of this painting is a WikiArt page ("Girl and Cat", c.1881-82, private collection, no dimensions) and a Wikidata item with zero references built from that page; no museum, catalogue raisonné, sale record or dimensions confirm the object, and the entry's 'Private Collection, Paris', '65 x 54 cm' and 'No 0146' are unsupported.

original.title: Young Girl with a Cat (Jeune fille au chat)
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: A blonde young girl with rosy cheeks cradles a patient domestic cat against her shoulder, wrapping her arms securely around its soft body. Renoir renders the child's flowing locks and striped dress with feathery, broken Impressionist strokes, while defining the cat's resting paws and alert ears with warm ochres and creamy whites. The feline looks placidly toward the spectator, completely yielding to the affectionate embrace. Look closely at the young girl's embrace to find the patient domestic cat cradled against her shoulder.
original.context: Painted in 1882 following Renoir's Italian journey, this work reflects his growing interest in classical linear structure while retaining Impressionist luminosity and softness. Renoir painted numerous portraits of bourgeois children with companion animals to capture childhood innocence.
original.title_eng: Young Girl with a Cat
original.feline_symbolism: The cradled cat personifies gentle trust, domestic security, and the instinctive empathy between young children and family pets.

title: Lady with a Broom Chasing a Cat with Fish
title_eng: Lady with a Broom Chasing a Cat with Fish
reason: The image is a 2024 phone snapshot by a Wikimedia user of an unidentified Kalighat-style painting with no location, owner, date or museum record, so the claimed V&A object ('No 0551', 42.5 x 27 cm) cannot be confirmed and the id describes a different subject (babu as a cat playing the sitar).

original.title: Lady with a Broom Chasing a Cat with Fish
original.description: An elegantly adorned Bengali housewife raises a whisk broom overhead in anger, confronting a spotted cat that scurries across the floor clutching a stolen fish in its jaws. Rendered with bold undulating brush strokes, the woman is depicted in a diaphanous silver-bordered sari with traditional bangles and nose ring. The startled cat looks back over its shoulder with dilated pupils, twisting its spotted body in a frantic sprint. Look closely at the lower left corner beneath the woman's silver-trimmed sari to find the spotted cat scrambling away with a fish clamped in its mouth.
original.context: Kalighat paintings of domestic strife and kitchen theft captured the daily dramas of colonial-era Bengali households with sharp humor and social commentary. The clash between domestic authority and the unrepentant feline thief became a favored comic trope in nineteenth-century Calcutta bazaars.
original.title_eng: Lady with a Broom Chasing a Cat with Fish
original.medium: Watercolor and silver on paper
original.feline_symbolism: The kitchen-raiding cat personifies opportunistic audacity, domestic disruption, and the irrepressible wild instinct persisting within urban domesticity.

title: Smiling Cat (Chat souriant)
reason: The image is a 2011 visitor photo captioned only 'Émile Gallé, faïence, Musée Charles de Bruyères (Remiremont)' and categorised as Gallé tableware and vases, with no cat category; nothing confirms that the object shown is a cat, and the claimed Musée de l'École de Nancy 'Smiling Cat' with glass eyes is not supported.

original.title: Smiling Cat (Chat souriant)
original.description: Sculpted in tin-glazed earthenware with vivid sulfur-yellow enamel, this seated domestic cat sports an exaggerated, human-like grin and piercing inset green glass eyes. Gallé adorns the feline coat with whimsical blue rococo cartouches, delicate lace cuffs, and sprigs of stylized floral sprays painted in cobalt blue. The rounded forms and smooth, reflective glaze epitomize the playful animalier production of the École de Nancy.
original.context: Produced at Gallé's family faience workshops in Nancy around 1885, these life-size ceramic cats were fashionable parlor guardians placed beside drawing-room fireplaces and bay windows across France and Great Britain. Gallé drew inspiration from historic 18th-century Lunéville and Saint-Clément ceramics, reinterpreting folk whimsy through the lens of early Art Nouveau.
original.title_eng: Smiling Cat
original.medium: Tin-glazed earthenware (faience) with inset green glass eyes
original.collection: Musée de l'École de Nancy, Nancy, France
original.submovement: École de Nancy Art Nouveau Faience
original.feline_symbolism: The uncanny human smile and hypnotic glass gaze project a benign esoteric mischief, embodying the domestic feline as an ironic, benevolent household spirit.

title: A Cat Orchestra (A Kitten's Concert)
reason: The image is the well-known internet montage of six unrelated Louis Wain cat pictures (Commons: 'Six paintings of cats... increasing degree of abstractedness', dated 'between 1886 and 1939', sourced from a blog), not a single work; the 'Cat Orchestra, 1886' title, medium, dimensions and British Library location are not supported.

original.title: A Cat Orchestra (A Kitten's Concert)
original.medium: Pen, black India ink, and grey wash on paper
original.description: Six anthropomorphic kittens stand upright upon a makeshift wooden stage, earnestly playing miniature violins, flutes, and sheet music with comically furrowed brows. Wain utilizes crisp India ink hatching and delicate grey washes to articulate their fluffy kitten coats and oversized, expressive eyes. The composition captures the artist's earliest breakthrough in humanizing feline behavior without abandoning naturalistic kitten proportions.
original.context: Published in the mid-1880s following Wain's marriage to Emily Richardson, this drawing predates his monumental eleven-panel spread for The Illustrated London News Christmas edition of 1886. Wain began drawing cats to amuse Emily during her terminal illness with breast cancer, using their rescue cat Peter as his patient studio model.
original.title_eng: A Cat Orchestra (A Kitten's Concert)
original.feline_symbolism: The musical performance transforms ordinary domestic mischief into refined Victorian social mimicry, celebrating the kitten as an endearing reflection of human vanity.

title: Cat Catching a Mouse (from Kyōsai Gadan)
reason: Duplicate: the image is 'Cat art detail, from MET DT5300 (cropped)', a crop of the Met photograph DT5300 of Kyōsai's 'Cat Catching a Frog' (14.76.61.20), which is already entry ex-375-...; the claimed 'Cat Catching a Mouse from Kyōsai Gadan' is not what the image shows.

original.title: Cat Catching a Mouse (from Kyōsai Gadan)
original.description: With explosive graphic dynamism, Kyōsai portrays a tortoiseshell cat pinning a terrified rodent beneath its splayed front claws while curling its back in fierce triumph. The feline's whiskers bristle, its ears flatten defensively, and its wide golden eyes gleam with manic intensity, executed with bravura calligraphic brushwork translated into woodcut. Behind the struggling predator sits a miniature potted bonsai, accentuating the chaotic rupture of cultivated domestic order.
original.context: Kawanabe Kyōsai was late nineteenth-century Japan's most inventive and technically dazzling virtuoso, celebrated for his wild spontaneous caricatures (*kyōga*) and piercing social satires. Trained in both traditional Kanō academic painting and popular Utagawa ukiyo-e, Kyōsai captured animal movements with razor-sharp kinetic accuracy and irreverent humor.
original.title_eng: Cat Catching a Mouse
original.medium: Woodblock-printed book illustration; ink and light color on paper
original.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
original.submovement: Meiji Era Kyōsai School Expressive Woodblock Printmaking
original.feline_symbolism: The cat catching the mouse represents untamable predatory prowess, triumphant natural justice, and the visceral vitality of the streetwise survivor.

original.title: The Curious Kittens in the Sewing Basket
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: Four fluffy kittens create delightful domestic havoc within a wicker sewing basket, becoming comically ensnared in unraveling spools of scarlet and sky-blue silk embroidery thread. Adam captures the chaotic tumble of soft paws and twisting tails with virtuoso brushwork, contrasting the smooth sheen of silk thread with the prickly wicker basket and downy fur. One adventurous kitten balances precariously on the basket's rim with arched tail, while another bats intently at a dangling wooden needle case.
original.context: Acquired for the Neue Pinakothek in Munich, this painting exemplifies Adam's signature motif of domestic curiosity meeting female handicraft, a favorite theme in Victorian and Wilhelmine parlor art.
original.title_eng: The Curious Kittens in the Sewing Basket
original.feline_symbolism: A lighthearted celebration of playful domestic chaos, innocent mischief, and the irresistible feline attraction to moving threads.

original.title: A Prowl on the Table (Un petit tour sur la table)
original.medium: Oil on panel
original.description: A long-haired calico queen cautiously explores a high-bourgeois tea table, delicately stepping between porcelain teacups and a silver tea service while her kitten peers over the rim of a linen-covered tray. Ronner-Knip demonstrates her peerless mastery of surface textures, juxtaposing the soft, downy brushwork of the cat's fur against the metallic gleam of chased silver and the translucent glaze of bone china. The cat's poised, cautious gait captures the quintessential feline balance of brazen inquisitiveness and poised physical grace.
original.context: Highly prized by late Victorian and Belgian collectors, Ronner-Knip's tea table genre scenes reflected the elevation of long-haired Angoras and Persians as symbols of refined domestic luxury and parlor indulgence.
original.title_eng: A Prowl on the Table
original.feline_symbolism: Emblem of domestic privilege, refined curiosity, and the delicate harmony of animal instinct within civilized bourgeois interiors.

original.title: By the Fireplace (Bij de haard)
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: Before an ornate marble mantelpiece, a magnificent long-haired Angora mother cat dozes peacefully on a plush Persian hearth rug, while two adventurous kittens tumble across the brass fender and play with fallen kindling. Ronner-Knip captures the radiant, flickering warmth of the hearthside with rich glazes, illuminating the amber highlights in the mother's fur and the glittering reflections on polished brass andirons. The composition epitomizes the Victorian cult of the domestic hearth, where the cat reigned supreme as the living symbol of fireside comfort.
original.context: The hearth was the sacred epicenter of the Victorian home; paintings of cats curled beside the fireplace were widely interpreted as emblems of domestic contentment, moral safety, and shelter from the harsh external world.

original.title: Naturalistic Study of a Seated Tabby
original.medium: Charcoal, graphite, and grey wash with white heightening on paper
original.description: In a departure from comic anthropomorphism, this sober observational drawing portrays a domestic shorthair cat seated upright in three-quarter view. Wain uses dense charcoal shading, stump blending, and crisp white chalk heightening to render the muscular contours of the chest and the dense texture of the striped coat. The cat's watchful, unblinking gaze and erect posture demonstrate the artist's foundational academic skill in animal anatomy.
original.context: Before developing his famous caricatural style, Wain trained rigorously at the West London School of Art and worked as an academic animal draftsman for agricultural journals. This early naturalistic drawing proves that Wain's subsequent stylized cats rested upon a bedrock of formidable anatomical knowledge.
original.title_eng: Naturalistic Study of a Seated Tabby
original.feline_symbolism: The unadorned, realistic tabby represents the quiet dignity and self-contained mystery of the domestic animal in its pure, natural state.

original.title: Mischief and Repose (The Artist's Studio)
original.medium: Oil on canvas
original.description: Upon a luxurious velvet-draped settee in a Victorian drawing room, a regal white mother cat rests peacefully with heavy-lidded eyes, while her three unruly kittens tumble across an embroidered silk cushion and unspool a skein of blue knitting yarn. Ronner-Knip constructs the complex composition with dazzling technical virtuosity, contrasting the maternal cat's serene immobility with the acrobatic kinetics of her kittens. The silky textures of the felines' coats, the tactile nap of the velvet upholstery, and the gilded woodwork of the settee showcase the artist at the height of her international fame.
original.context: Presented to the British National Gallery of British Art (now Tate Britain) in 1893 by prominent collector Henry Tate, this masterwork solidified Ronner-Knip's canonical reputation in Victorian Britain as the peerless chronicler of feline life.
original.title_eng: Mischief and Repose
original.feline_symbolism: The dual nature of the domestic cat—combining absolute, tranquil repose with sudden, spirited mischief—symbolizing the balance of peace and vitality in the ideal home.
