original.title: Ovinnik (The Barn Cat Spirit)
original.description: Ivan Bilibin’s evocative graphic illustration captures the Ovinnik, the Slavic hearth and threshing-barn spirit manifested in the form of a wild, disheveled black cat dwelling beside the grain-drying furnace. Rendered in crisp graphic contours influenced by traditional Russian lubok prints and Japanese woodblocks, the feline spirit glares with incandescent orange eyes from the shadowed barn rafters. In Slavic pagan folklore, the Ovinnik protected dried grain from vermin and winter frost, but would spitefully burn down the barn if farmers worked on holy days or neglected hearth rituals.
original.context: Celebrated for illustrating Russian skazki (fairy tales), Bilibin synthesized traditional Slavic peasant folklore with Northern Art Nouveau aesthetics under the patron circle of Mir Iskusstva (World of Art).
original.title_eng: Ovinnik (The Barn Cat Spirit)
original.medium: Ink and watercolor on paper
original.submovement: Russian Art Nouveau Illustration & Slavic Folklore
original.feline_symbolism: The primordial domestic guardian of harvest and fire, embodying both agricultural protection and the fiery peril of offended house spirits.

original.title: The Cat Club Meeting (Katzenklub)
original.medium: Gouache, watercolor, and black ink on paperboard
original.description: Around an oak boardroom table, an assembly of grave cat dignitaries in starched collars, spectacles, and cravats debate club business with theatrical pomposity. Wain emphasizes the contrasting personalities through expressive feline postures: a bulldog-faced British Shorthair bangs a gavel while a sleek Siamese secretary scribbles notes with an ink quill. Fine brushwork and warm gouache glazes delineate the polished wood paneling and Victorian clubroom appointments.
original.context: Wain drew directly from his own executive experience as President of the National Cat Club from 1898 to 1911. He presided over formal committee meetings in London hotel suites and clubs, using this humorous composition to poke gentle fun at himself and his fellow cat fanciers.
original.title_eng: The Cat Club Meeting (Katzenklub)

original.description: Masterfully carved from a single piece of natural banded Siberian agate, this miniature sculpture depicts a domestic cat seated in alert repose with tail wrapped neatly around its paws. The lapidary skillfully oriented the raw gemstone so that its undulating honey, brown, and cream strata mimic the natural dorsal striping of a tabby coat. original.title: Cat in the Moonlight (Chat au clair de lune)
original.medium: Color lithograph on wove paper
original.description: Bathed in the cool silver radiance of a full moon, a solitary black cat prowls across the sloping tiles of a Paris roof. Steinlen creates a nocturnal chiaroscuro using velvety midnight blues, inky blacks, and silvery highlights on the cat's arched spine and whiskers. original.description: Rendered in energetic crosshatched India ink, the smirking anthropomorphic tabby Fritz rests his arms nonchalantly within a circular medallion, gazing slyly from beneath heavy, hooded eyelids. original.description: At the base of an imposing nine-meter commemorative civic column, three life-size sculpted white cats sit sentinel, with the central feline raising its right paw in a formal civic salute. Local legend attributes the city's name to James Brooke, the first White Rajah of Sarawak, who reportedly pointed to the settlement and asked its name, receiving the Malay word for cat from a confused local.

original.title: Cat Sitting On Himself (The Modern Cat Sìth in Repose)
original.description: Resting upright upon a bedspread in an uncannily humanoid posture, a muscular brown mackerel tabby cat gazes steadily forward with piercing green-gold eyes, its hind legs splayed and forepaws draped over its belly. Lynne R. Lawrie's intimate flash photography accentuates the bold black transverse striping across the feline's flanks and the soft cream underbelly fur exposed in its relaxed pose. The photograph captures the modern domestic cat's idiosyncratic physical flexibility while evoking the ancient Celtic tradition of the Cat Sìth—the mythical fairy cat of the Scottish Highlands reputed to assume humanlike poses and intelligence.
original.context: In Gaelic Highland folklore, the Cat Sìth (Cat Sidhe in Ireland) was conceived not as an ordinary animal but as a supernatural fairy creature or witch possessing the power to transform nine times. During the traditional Feill Fhadraig (Late Wake), mourners held vigil day and night to prevent a Cat Sìth from leaping over the unburied corpse, which folklore held would steal the departed soul before the gods could claim it; similarly, saucers of milk were left outside on Samhain night to earn the creature's domestic blessing.

original.medium: Digital color photograph
original.feline_symbolism: The Cat Sìth personifies the liminal threshold between domestic animal and supernatural spirit in Celtic mythology, representing nocturnal mystery, soul guardianship, and the ancient fear of feline otherworldly intelligence.

original.title: Thor Lifts the Cat (Jörmungandr Disguised as the Giant Cat)
original.description: The cat in this picture has already dropped its disguise. Frølich shows the giant king Útgarða-Loki's house cat as what it really is, Jörmungandr: a scaly body arched into a vault over Thor's head, clawed feet planted on the ground, the head low at bottom left. Thor, bearded and bare-chested, pushes up with one straining arm, and the beast hardly notices. In the Prose Edda, however hard Thor heaves, the cat simply arches its back until only one paw leaves the floor. A carved frieze of small figures runs across the top. A sheet from the series at the Royal Danish Academy measures 29.2 × 24.2 cm.
original.context: Lorenz Frølich (1820–1908) was a Copenhagen-born etcher and illustrator who spent long years in Paris and Rome and became a professor at the Royal Danish Academy in 1877. Norse myth was a lifelong subject: he illustrated Oehlenschläger's Nordens Guder and Edda poems, and his cartoons later became tapestries for Copenhagen City Hall. This image belongs to Gjøgleriet i Utgard (The Trickery at Utgard), published in 1872. Fun fact: the cat is a fake. Útgarða-Loki later admits it was the World Serpent Jörmungandr under an illusion, so the one paw Thor raised was a tremendous feat.
original.title_eng: Thor Lifts the Cat
original.medium: Etching
original.feline_symbolism: In the saga the cat is a disguise for the serpent that circles the world, so its stubborn weight is the weight of the earth itself.
original.image_credit: Lorenz Frølich · Scanned by Haukur from a reprint in the illustrated 2002 Prose Edda edition by Gudrun. Originally published in Gjøgleriet i Utgard (1872).

original.title: The Cat (El Gato)
original.medium: Oil on cardboard
original.collection: Museo Nacional de Artes Visuales (MNAV), Montevideo
original.description: No cat turns up in this patio, despite the title. What fills the oil on cardboard, a large sheet for that support at 70 × 100 cm, is a party: a man in a red neckerchief and white trousers faces a woman in a pale blue polka-dot dress, a seated man plays guitar, and women in yellow, white and blue line the pink walls under a vine-hung arcade. Two dogs wander through. Figari almost always painted on board, with quick, thin, broken touches, and worked from memory, so the scene is remembered, assembled from decades of patios, not posed.
original.context: Pedro Figari (1861–1938) was a lawyer who defended the poor, a member of Parliament and head of the Ateneo de Montevideo before he turned to painting full time in 1921, at sixty, in Buenos Aires. From 1925 he worked in Paris, painting Uruguayan life from memory: candombe dances, criollo patios, gauchos. El gato, dated around 1927, belongs to the Museo Nacional de Artes Visuales in Montevideo. Fun fact: he described his own project as reconstructing rather than documenting the Uruguayan scene, which makes a remembered cat entirely on brand.

title: The Kaleidoscope Cats (Maclay Progression Series)
reason: Visual pass: the image is a modern 2x3 montage of six separate Louis Wain pictures, not one object; the claimed Bethlem/Guttmann-Maclay series of eight cannot be matched to it. Same case as the purged louis-wain-wain-cats-6-1886.

original.title: The Kaleidoscope Cats (Maclay Progression Series)
original.medium: Gouache and watercolor on paper (series of eight studies)
original.collection: Bethlem Museum of the Mind / Guttmann-Maclay Collection
original.description: Read as a strip, the pictures go from a cat that looks like a cat to a cat that looks like a textile. Early in the sequence the animal has fur, a body and a stare; further along, its outline breaks into repeating, increasingly symmetrical ornament until the face is a hub in a pattern. That visual drift is exactly why the pictures were put in this order, and the order is the problem (see below). The image attached to this entry is a modern montage of six of the pictures, not one object.
original.context: In 1939 the psychiatrist Walter Maclay found eight undated Wain pictures in a London shop and arranged them in "an assumed chronological order to demonstrate the progression of the schizophrenic mind". The sequence, later called the Kaleidoscope Cats, went into psychology textbooks for decades. It now sits in the Guttmann-Maclay Collection at Bethlem Museum of the Mind, which holds several of the eight, including III, IV and VII. The catch, as Wellcome's 2020 article puts it, is that there was "no evidence to support this ordering". Bethlem's own director has called the sequence purely speculative, and Wain was still painting ordinary comic cats at Napsbury at the same time.

original.title_original: Studio per la Madonna del gatto (Verso)
original.medium: Pen and brown ink with brown wash over stylus underdrawing
original.description: Turn the sheet over and the same group appears flipped left to right, because Leonardo worked it out partly by tracing through the paper. The Virgin, the Child and the cat are set down again in pen and brown ink, with brown wash pooled in the shadows. Finestre sull'Arte points out that here the cat has moved to the right and rears up on its hind legs, the pose Leonardo also tried on a sheet now in Bayonne, so the reverse is a second experiment rather than a mere ghost of the front.
original.context: This is the back of the British Museum's small Leonardo sheet (13 × 9.4 cm), drawn in Florence around 1478–81 as one of about six studies of the Virgin and Child with a cat. The museum describes the verso as the same subject in reverse, drawn in pen and brown ink with brown wash over stylus. None of these ideas reached a finished painting. The sheet was bought from Giovanni Battista Cavalcaselle, the art historian who did much to put Italian painting in order for English readers. Fun fact: the mirror-image relationship between the two sides is visible simply by holding the sheet against the light.

title: Gallo-Roman Funerary Stele of Laetus's Daughter Holding a Cat
title_eng: Gallo-Roman Funerary Stele of Laetus's Daughter Holding a Cat
reason: Depicted animal is archaeozoologically and curatorially identified as a dog/puppy (chiot), not a felid (Nuovo & Zych 2023; Musée d'Aquitaine official catalogue for inv. 60.1.75). Violates curatorial rule 1 (cats/felids only).

original.title: Gallo-Roman Funerary Stele of Laetus's Daughter Holding a Cat
original.title_original: Stèle funéraire de la fille de Laetus avec son chat
original.medium: Carved local limestone grave relief with traces of polychromy
original.dimensions: Height: 125 cm; Width: 46 cm; Depth: 24 cm
original.description: The cat is held right against the girl's chest, its round head and pricked ears facing out between her hands, so the two faces stack one above the other. It is a child's tombstone, and the sculptor gave her what a child would have cared about: a pet to hold and, lower down beside her, a rooster to chase. The cat is unmistakable, a real household animal held close rather than a symbol floating in the background. The inscription runs down the left edge, opening with the formula D(is) M(anibus), 'to the spirits of the dead', then naming her father, Laetus, with PAT for pater.
original.context: The stele was found in Bordeaux, Roman Burdigala, and is now in the Musée d'Aquitaine. Its inscription is catalogued as CIL XIII 787 (also AE 2003, 1167); it reads D(is) M(anibus) / Laetus / pat(er) and then breaks off, so the girl's own name is lost. The monument is the starting point of Catherine Johns's article 'The Tombstone of Laetus' Daughter: Cats in Gallo-Roman Sculpture' (Britannia 34, 2003), which uses it to survey how domestic cats appear in the art of Roman Gaul. Fun fact: Johns opens by complaining that histories of the cat 'normally concentrate on ancient Egypt'; this small grave relief is her counter-argument.
original.title_eng: Gallo-Roman Funerary Stele of Laetus's Daughter Holding a Cat

title: Cat and Kittens Drinking Milk from a Saucer
artist: After Gottfried Mind (lithograph associated with Joseph Brodtmann)
collection: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C.
description: A big patched mother cat and a single striped kitten drink from the same saucer, heads almost touching, the kitten's front paw on the rim. The digitiser speaks of kittens, but this impression has only one. A saucer is the oldest trick in the cat painter's book: it pulls every animal toward one point, so even this mismatched pair becomes a composition. The mother's heavy body nearly dwarfs the kitten, and her tail flicks out behind. In the lithograph the milk is just untouched white paper, and the darker fur around it does the work of making it look wet.
context: Gottfried Mind (1768–1814), the Bern artist known as 'the Raphael of Cats', drew this kind of everyday scene over and over, and lithographs after his designs, associated with Joseph Brodtmann (1787–1862), made them affordable after his death. This sheet is in the Library of Congress and was digitally enhanced by rawpixel. Fun fact: the Library also holds a near-identical subject, 'Domestic cat and kitten drinking milk from a saucer', signed 'CF' and numbered 3, so this cat and her saucer may appear twice in the catalogue.
title_eng: Cat and Kittens Drinking Milk from a Saucer
submovement: Reproductive lithographs after Gottfried Mind (Joseph Brodtmann)
image_credit: Rawpixel · Own work

Same mother, same patches, same kitten and saucer; the LoC original is the better-sourced, public-domain version. Its source_url (item/2012645544) also duplicates entry 21's.

title: Soviet Soldiers with a Cat in Stalingrad
title_original: Советские бойцы с кошкой на руках в Сталинграде
license: © Estate of Yakov Ryumkin, all rights reserved
description: A tabby-and-white cat stares straight into the lens from the arms of a smiling Soviet soldier in Stalingrad, a city being fought over street by street. A second soldier reaches across in a padded glove to stroke it, and a third grins from behind, all three in steel helmets, a submachine gun slung across the front. Behind them rises a burnt-out wreck of girders and a great wheel. The picture is a straight black-and-white press photograph by a frontline photojournalist, and the cat is the only thing in it not in uniform. The original caption simply calls it "a cat".
context: Yakov Ryumkin (1913-1986) photographed the battle of Stalingrad for the Soviet press, and this frame, captioned "Soviet soldiers with a cat in their arms in Stalingrad", is dated 1942. It circulates through the Russian war-photo archive Voennyi Albom, which credits the image to photo.may9.ru and the information to the culture ministry's portal. Online, the picture is often linked to Mourka, a Stalingrad cat said to have carried messages between Soviet positions. Nothing in the photograph's own record supports that identification, so the cat should be treated as anonymous; the Mourka story belongs to the legend, not to this negative.
title_eng: Soviet Soldiers with a Cat in Stalingrad
collection: State Historical Museum / RIA Novosti Archive, Moscow
image_credit: © Estate of Yakov Ryumkin. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from waralbum.ru and is not stored on this site.
reason: No holding-institution record: source is waralbum.ru, a website, not a museum or archive. Collection 'State Historical Museum / RIA Novosti Archive' and inventory 'RIA-84920' are unverified inventions, and the photo is only loosely tied to the Mourka legend. Fails rule 2 (and drifts toward rule 1's folklore exclusion).

title: Minneke Poes (Ypres Kattenstoet Giant Festival Effigy)
description: Minneke Poes is a giant: like other Flemish processional giants she is a towering costumed figure with an oversized head, here a white cat's with rouged lips and a black feathered topknot, carried through the streets of Ypres by bearers hidden inside. She wears a red ruffled jacket over a black bodice and a vast quilted white skirt, paws held out wide, a white tail curling up behind her. She walks in the Kattenstoet as the showpiece of the parade, beside the tomcat giant Cieper. Giants are made to be read from far off, so the face is simple. Watch her in motion: giants sway and turn rather than walk.
context: Frans Van Immerseel, who also designed the tomcat Cieper, designed Minneke Poes in 1960; a Dutch Wikipedia caption says the giant was made that year for Zwevegem and given to Ypres in 1971. The Kattenstoet itself began modestly in 1938, when celluloid toy cats were thrown from the belfry of the Cloth Hall, and became a full procession on 6 March 1955; it now runs every three years in May. It recalls an older custom, recorded from at least the 1590s, of throwing live cats from the tower. Fun fact: the throwing still happens, but the jester now lobs plush cats, and the crowd fights to catch one.
title_eng: Minneke Poes (Ypres Festival of the Cats Giant Effigy)
medium: Painted papier-mâché, wood, cane armature, and tailored textile gown
collection: Stad Ieper Collection / Ypres Guild of Giants, Ypres, Belgium

title: Orangey as 'Cat' with Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany's
description: A ginger tabby, the real subject of this entry, rears up on his hind legs, tail stretched straight out, reaching for whatever Audrey Hepburn holds. As Holly Golightly she kneels barefoot in a white robe, sleep mask pushed up into her hair, a bowl on the floor beside them. The image is a cropped frame from Paramount's 1961 trailer for Breakfast at Tiffany's, so what you see is soft film colour and lighting set up for a moving camera, not a posed studio portrait. Holly calls him simply Cat, a running joke about her refusal to own anything. He was played by a trained animal actor with a reputation.
context: The cat was played by Orangey, the stage name of several red tabbies owned and trained by Frank Inn, who said he paid 25 dollars for the first. Orangey won a PATSY award for Rhubarb (1951) and a second for Breakfast at Tiffany's, the only cat to win two. He also appeared in This Island Earth, The Incredible Shrinking Man and The Diary of Anne Frank. Studio publicity treated him as one cat, though he had about a dozen stand-ins. Fun fact: a studio executive called him the world's meanest cat; he scratched actors and sometimes ran off after a take, and Inn once posted guard dogs at the studio gate to stop him escaping.
title_eng: Orangey as 'Cat' with Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany's
collection: Paramount Pictures Studio Archive / Academy Film Archive, Beverly Hills

title: Mark Twain with Kitten
description: A tabby kitten sits cupped in both of Mark Twain's hands, and he bends his white head to look down at it with a cigar clamped in his mouth. He sits on a small boulder in his white suit on a sloping lawn under trees. The kitten is the small grey knot at the centre of a picture that is otherwise all white cloth and white hair. It is a press photograph, not a studio confection: a commercial firm made it to be reproduced in newspapers, and it worked.
context: Underwood & Underwood, the New York photographic agency, took this portrait in 1907, three years before Twain's death. A dealer's listing says it became known as 'I Always Had a Fondness for Kittens' after the New York Times ran it that year; the copy on Wikimedia Commons came from the Times photo archive. Twain liked the image enough to sign prints: one sold at RR Auction carries the inscription 'To Mrs. Kate D. Riggs, with the love of Mark Twain, Jan. 14/08'. Fun fact: his cats had names like Sour Mash, Apollinaris, Zoroaster and Blatherskite, which he claimed were chosen to give children practice with hard words.
collection: Mark Twain House & Museum, Hartford, Connecticut / Library of Congress

title: Three Cats (Drei Katzen)
description: Three cats gather round a white saucer of milk: a long-haired black-and-white cat sits upright at left, one drinks with its head down in the foreground, and a third lies at the back, watching the drinker. The canvas is 50 by 64 cm, signed 'Fr. Marc' at lower left. This is Marc before the blue horses, and the interest is in how three animal bodies fit together as one shape around that bright oval of saucer. Marc returned to cats again and again over the next four years, and this is one of the earliest canvases in that run.
context: Franz Marc (1880-1916) trained at the Munich Academy and went to Paris in 1903 and 1907, where he felt a strong affinity with Van Gogh. Around 1908-09 he was still working out his animal painting; the bright primary colour and near-Cubist forms that made his name came only from the winter of 1910-11, when, in Morgan Meis's phrase, he 'became an artist'. This canvas is catalogued in Hoberg and Jansen's catalogue raisonné (2004) and its present whereabouts are unknown, which is not unusual for Marc's early oils.

title: Cat Basket
description: Two cats, not one: a calico curled tight inside a woven basket, green eyes just open over its own flank, and a tortoiseshell in the foreground, seen from behind, reaching up toward a green toy dangling on a stick among scattered yellow leaves. Oil on canvas, 58 by 69 cm, from 1909. The basket is a gift to a painter, a ready-made oval that frames one body inside the frame, and its pale weave sets off the patched fur. Read together, the pair is a little before-and-after of cat life, one asleep and one at play, treated at full easel size by a painter taking animals seriously.
context: Franz Marc (1880-1916) studied at the Munich Academy from 1900 and visited Paris in 1903 and 1907; his animal painting was still developing in 1909, and the bright primary colour and almost Cubist forms of his famous work came after the winter of 1910-11. Cat Basket is recorded in Hoberg and Jansen's 2004 catalogue raisonné of his paintings, and PubHist lists its present whereabouts as unknown. Cats run all through his work of 1909-12, from this basket to Cats on a Red Cloth and The White Cat of 1912.

title: Two Cats (Zwei Katzen)
description: Two black-and-white cats lie curled one above the other, heads down and backs rounded, their patched coats echoed by the swelling dark and light shapes of the ground around them. They fill a tall 98 × 74 cm surface, a substantial size for an animal picture with no people and no story. Marc signed it at upper left, "Marc", as he did on the larger canvases he meant to show. With no setting to speak of, the picture is about how two bodies fit against each other: the lower cat's spine runs parallel to the upper one's, and a white tail sweeps out along the bottom like a reflection.
context: Marc painted this in 1911, the year he co-founded Der Blaue Reiter with Wassily Kandinsky and began giving animals the central place that human figures held for most of his colleagues. He thought animals offered a purer way into nature than people did. The painting's present whereabouts are unknown, and the main record of it is the reproduction in the 2004 catalogue raisonné by Annegret Hoberg and Isabelle Jansen. Fun fact: in 1936–37 the Nazi regime ordered around 130 of Marc's works removed from German museums; whether this picture was among them is not stated in the sources I could open.

title: Dingo (illustrated book by Octave Mirbeau, with 55 etchings by Pierre Bonnard)
artist_dates: French, Fontenay-aux-Roses 1867–1947 Le Cannet
medium: Etching on laid paper (unbound book, 55 plates)
collection: Petit Palais, Musée des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris
description: In Mirbeau's novel, Miche is a three-month-old kitten whom the dog Dingo more or less raises: he sleeps with her in the same basket, guards her, carries her by the tail and takes her head in his mouth while she trusts him completely. She does not appear on the wrapper, though. There Bonnard's scribbled needle gives us Dingo alone, seen from behind, sitting and looking away, under the title in red. The unbound copy in the Petit Palais holds all 55 etched plates on laid paper, published by Ambroise Vollard in 1924, in a stack 38.5 × 28.4 cm and 4 cm thick.
context: Octave Mirbeau's Dingo (1913) is a satirical fable built around his own dog, who died in 1901; Mirbeau was too ill to finish it, and Léon Werth wrote the last chapters from his notes. Ambroise Vollard later published it with 55 etchings by Pierre Bonnard. The Petit Palais copy (PPL41) came with the bequest of Dr Maurice Girardin in 1953. Fun fact: Mirbeau's narrator calls the dog-and-kitten friendship unusual because the two belong to "races ennemies", which turns the usual cat-and-dog joke on its head.
feline_symbolism: In the novel Miche is the one creature Dingo protects, a counterweight to the dog's predatory 'law of murder'.

title: Poster Design with Cat (From 'Posters in Miniature')
medium: Halftone reproduction in the book Posters in Miniature (New York: R. H. Russell, 1896)
description: A Steinlen cat poster shrunk to pocket size: the La Bodinière exhibition poster, its black cat sitting tall in profile behind a curled calico, reproduced with the caption 'STEINLEN' beneath. This is page 235 of Posters in Miniature, a small New York book of 1896 that reproduced posters from France, England, Germany and America in black and white for collectors. The orange lettering of the original turns to pale grey here, nearly vanishing, while the black cat survives untouched, which is a useful test of a poster design: Steinlen's cat still reads at a few centimetres high.
context: Posters in Miniature was published in 1896 by Robert Howard Russell in New York, at the height of the poster-collecting craze. Edward Penfield, the leading American poster designer, wrote the introduction and Percival Pollard the foreword; Pollard pitched it as a handy pictorial survey for the amateur collector. The book also included what it called the most complete set of portraits of poster designers yet published. Penfield's introduction contains a line that suits Steinlen's cats rather well: 'A poster should tell its story at once; a design that needs study is not a poster, no matter how well it is executed.' The scanned copy belongs to the Getty Research Institute.
title_original: Dessin d'affiche au chat (Posters in Miniature)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
reason: Not an original work: the image is a page crop of a small halftone reproduction of Steinlen's La Bodinière poster in the 1896 book Posters in Miniature (Internet Archive scan). The same design is already in the catalogue as steinlen-exposition-la-bodiniere-1894 (BnF original), so this is a duplicate; and 'Getty Research Institute (Internet Archive scan)' is a scan, not an institutional object record.

title: Carol Singing Cats
medium: Watercolour, gouache, pen and pencil on paper
description: Eight cats carol in the snow outside a row of half-timbered houses, with full kit: cello, flute, trumpet, a big brass horn and a drum, one musician sprawled flat beneath it. From an upper window at left a cat empties a jug on the band while a mouse goes flying, and two cats in the distance let fly with snowballs. Wain's cats perform a human custom with complete seriousness, and get the human reception. Watercolour, gouache, pen and pencil share one sheet of about 15 by 22 inches (roughly 38 by 56 cm), an original drawing rather than one of the printed copies through which most people met his cats.
context: Christmas was part of Wain's cat world from the start: 'A Kitten's Christmas Party', his first drawing of anthropomorphised cats, ran in the Illustrated London News in 1886 and showed 150 cats in eleven panels, and the Louis Wain Annual kept the seasonal market supplied from 1901. The present sheet is known only from an auction listing reproduced on Wikimedia Commons, with no date or owner recorded. Fun fact: in August 1925 a statement by H. G. Wells, read out on the BBC, said Wain 'invented a cat style, a cat society, a whole cat world'.

title: Conversation amongst Cats
artist_dates: German-Hungarian, 1872–1931
description: White on white on white: three long-haired cats hold what looks like a meeting at the edge of a patterned rug. The middle one stands with its plumed tail up and looks straight at us, as if it has the floor; the one at right sits facing it, and the third lies flat on the parquet at left, eyes half shut, taking no part. A green curtain shuts off the left side and a small upholstered stool stands behind, so this is a comfortable parlour, not a pantry or a barn. At 76 × 113 cm the canvas is generous for a cat picture, and the white coats carry the light across it.
context: Haarhausen-born Heyer moved to Budapest in 1896, became a Hungarian citizen in 1900 and earned the nickname 'Cat-Heyer' for his Turkish Angoras. This canvas is undated; Commons can say only 'by 1931'. It is in a private collection, and its photograph comes from a sale at the Vienna auction house Dorotheum. Fun fact: he also painted deer, hares, pheasants and chickens, and in 1919 published two children's books of verse.

title: Young Angora Cat (Junge Angorakatze)
artist_dates: German-Hungarian, 1872–1931
collection: Unknown (photograph from a 2006 flyer on the artist)
description: One young white Angora, as Heyer's title 'Junge Angorakatze' promises: no second cat, no basket. The kitten is caught mid-step, front paw reaching forward, rump high and plumed tail flagged straight up, its blue eyes fixed on something off to the right. Its pink-lined ears and nose are the only warm notes against a blue-green backdrop and a red-brown floor. The long white coat is the reason for the picture. It is a modest canvas, 40 × 50 cm, the kind of size suited to a painter who lived on commissioned cat portraits.
context: Hungary awarded Heyer the Count Andrássy Prize in 1911, and in 1915 he was appointed professor in Munich. A German by birth, he had moved to Budapest in 1896 and held his first exhibition there in 1906, and he stayed known as 'Cat-Heyer' for his Turkish Angoras. This painting is undated, and its photograph comes from a 2006 flyer about the artist by Regina Pfundt. Fun fact: when he died in Budapest in 1931 he received a state funeral at Kerepesi Cemetery.

title: Dog and Cat (Hund und Katze)
description: A white long-haired cat peers out from behind a tree trunk at upper left, round-eyed and perfectly still, while a white terrier with brown patches and a leather collar barks at it with its mouth wide open. That is everything the title 'Dog and Cat' promises. Heyer built his reputation on white long-haired cats, so the dog is the outsider in his usual world, and he places it on open grass while the cat keeps the tree between them. The 50 × 70 cm canvas gives the two animals room to keep their distance. Signed 'Heyer A.' lower left.
context: Not only cats: Heyer also painted deer, hares, pheasants, chickens and dogs, mostly his own dog Mucki. German-born, he moved to Budapest in 1896, became a Hungarian citizen in 1900 and exhibited in Weimar and Gotha in 1909. This canvas is undated and privately owned; its photograph comes from a sale at the Vienna auction house Dorotheum. Fun fact: despite the nickname 'Cat-Heyer', dogs run through his output too, and the terrier here is an outsider in a world of white Angoras.

title: The Last Move
medium: Oil on canvas (known only from a 1905 halftone reproduction)
collection: Unknown (copyright owned by Braun, Clément & Co., Paris, in 1905)
description: Four cats and a chess game. A tabby kitten pounces onto the board, scattering pieces across the tablecloth, a white kitten crouches behind it, a third peers down from the carved crest of the chair, and a big tabby-and-white cat sits at left watching like a referee. The title 'The Last Move' makes that pounce the decisive play. What survives online is the 1905 halftone plate from Women Painters of the World, page 279, headed 'Flemish School, Contemporary'. Chess pieces were a favourite Ronner prop, small enough to bat, topple and chase.
context: The plate credit reads 'reproduced from the original painting by permission of Messrs. Fun fact: the same book praises her daughter Alice Ronner as 'beyond dispute the foremost painter of still-life in Belgium'.

title: Her Favourite
collection: Private collection (Sotheby's London, The Russian Sale, 2006, lot 54)
description: Held at arm's length by a woman lying on her back across a white bed, a black cat with a white bib dangles in the air near the top of the picture; she smiles up at it, her bare legs crossed and kicked high. title: Two Friends (Zwei Freunde)
collection: Sold at Dorotheum, Vienna (lot 7201720); present owner unknown
description: A white long-haired cat with pale green eyes crouches on a striped red rug and stares straight at us, while a fawn pug sits upright beside it, looking off to the left with a worried black face. The two friends of the title are a cat and a dog, not two cats. Ronner-Knip painted them in oil on a wood panel, 48 by 62 cm, signed 'Henriette Ronner' at lower right. A panel takes paint smoothly, which suits the fine work that long white fur demands, and the dark carved table leg behind them makes the white glow. context: Joseph August Knip, a painter who went blind, gave his daughter her first lessons, and she ended up supporting the family. Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) was born in Amsterdam, moved to Brussels after her marriage in 1850 and narrowed her subjects to dogs and cats; from the 1870s she was best known for long-haired cats in bourgeois interiors. In later years she reportedly made paper models of the poses she wanted. This panel was offered at the Dorotheum in Vienna, and its date is only fixed as before her death in February 1909.

title: Mother Cat with Two Kittens

collection: Private collection (sold Lempertz, Cologne, 20 May 2023, lot 2289)

title: Cosmetic Vessel in the Shape of a Cat
title_original: Cosmetic Vessel in the Shape of a Cat
description: On a flat rectangular base, this cat sits bolt upright and holds its front legs straight, the stone pale and glossy, with a small round hole in its flank and one ear chipped. It is carved in the round from travertine (Egyptian alabaster) as a cosmetic jar. The eyes are rock crystal lined with copper, now gone green, so the stare still catches the light like a wet eye would. Tense and alert, it has what the Met calls the look of a hunter rather than the elegant aloofness seen in later cats.
context: Dated to the early Middle Kingdom, around 1990 to 1900 BCE, this jar was called by the Met the earliest-known three-dimensional representation of a cat in Egyptian art, adding that the cat first appears in painting and relief at the end of the Old Kingdom. It entered the collection in 1990 (accession 1990.59.1). Then the story changed. The Met's open-access API no longer returns the object, and an earlier check of the museum's record reported that it was restituted in April 2026, without naming the recipient, so its present home is unconfirmed.

title: Leda and the Swan
description: Almost lost in the shadows at lower left, a dark cat crouches at the foot of a wooden coop, taunting the duck shut inside it. Above it the maid leans over the coop with one hand on its bars. Leda reclines across the bed, naked but for pearls at her throat and in her hair, her hand on the swan that presses in from the right, and a small white dog scampers along the green cover at her feet. Red curtains sweep behind her, and a second cage hangs in the gloom at the back. Her body runs in one bright diagonal against the maid's opposite lean, a V that keeps the whole picture moving.
context: Restorations in 1988 and 1994 settled doubts about whether Tintoretto painted this himself, and most art historians now place it in the 1550s, though they do not fully agree. In the late eighteenth century it hung in the Orléans collection in Paris, then was bought in London by the Duke of Bridgewater; Paul Norton owned it in 1857, and Arturo De Noè Walker gave it to the Uffizi in 1895. Fun fact: the Uffizi owns a second version, from the Contini Bonacossi collection, whose servant was later cut away, and that mutilated canvas is probably the model for this one.

title: Cats Fighting in a Larder, with Loaves of Bread, a Dressed Lamb, Artichokes and Grapes
title_original: Dos gatos riñendo en una despensa
collection: Galerie Pierre Birtschansky, Paris (sold Christie's New York, 27 April 2017, lot 40A)
description: Broken into the larder, the cats have gone for each other instead of the food. One launches itself down from the window ledge, claws out and mouth open, while two more lock together on the tabletop at left, one flipped on its back and snarling up at the attacker. A fourth, ginger, peers in over the sill to watch. Around the scrap Snyders piles the goods: an overturned basket spilling loaves and oranges, scattered knives and forks, a dressed lamb draped over a copper cistern, artichokes, asparagus, grapes. It is a big panel, more than 90 by 100 centimetres.

Hoogendijk in Amsterdam in 1932, was sold in Stockholm in 1942 to a family who kept it for generations, and was auctioned at Christie's New York on 27 April 2017. Snyders (1579–1657), master in the Antwerp guild from 1602 and later its dean, made his name with market stalls, larders and animal fights, and supplied animals and still-life passages for Rubens. He often dropped live animals, cats especially, into still lifes to set the living against the inert. Commons now lists the picture with Galerie Pierre Birtschansky.

title: Cat Crouching on the Ledge of an Artist's Atelier
title_original: Kater op een vensterbank van een schildersatelier
description: A ginger-and-cream striped cat crouches in profile on a stone ledge, front paws stretched forward, eyes alert, watching something just outside the picture to the right while its long banded tail trails off the left end of the sill. Dou built the fur from countless tiny strokes with a brush of only a few hairs. A red curtain with violet highlights hangs from rings in the arched niche, and deep in the dark room behind, a painter works at his easel with a violin on the table beside him. The cat looks like a particular animal rather than a generic one; an 1859 catalogue went ahead and called it 'Master Dou's Housecat'.
context: 'GDou 1657' is the signature and date on this panel. It is one of only three known animal paintings by him and the only picture in which he shows an artist actually at work. The Leiden Collection reads the cat as Sight, following prints like Goltzius and Saenredam's Visus, and the curtain as a nod to Parrhasius, whose painted curtain fooled a rival; Dou was praised as the 'Dutch Parrhasius'. X-rays reveal a different first idea underneath: a young woman pouring from a jug, perhaps a mousetrap. The panel is reused Baltic oak. It was in the Dresden royal collection by 1722, returned to the House of Wettin in 1924, and bought by the Leiden Collection in 2006.
title_eng: Cat Crouching on the Ledge of an Artist's Atelier
feline_symbolism: The keen-eyed cat stands for Sight, the sense on which a painter of Dou's illusionism depends.

title: Cats with a Still Life of Marine Animals, Fruit and Vegetables
title_original: Katten bij een stilleven in een voorraadkamer
artist: Workshop of Jan van Kessel the Elder
submovement: Antwerp cabinet painting on copper (van Kessel workshop)
description: A white kitten peeks over the rim of a red earthenware pot, paws hooked on the edge, while a black-and-white cat at right makes off with a long silver fish clamped crosswise in its jaws. The French sale title, Deux chats jouant avec du poisson, gets straight to the point. Around them spill eels, red mullet, a spiny red crab, oysters, a salmon steak hung on the wall and a basket of pale grapes. It is painted in oil on a small copper plate, 23.5 by 31 centimetres, the hard, smooth support that van Kessel's shop favoured because it let fine brushwork stay crisp: individual scales, wet shell, single hairs of fur.
context: RKD catalogues this one as a workshop product of about 1665 to 1679, which means assistants carried out a composition the master devised. Jan van Kessel the Elder (1626–1679), grandson of Jan Brueghel the Elder, ran a busy Antwerp studio producing small, jewel-like animal and still-life pictures on copper for collectors' cabinets. It is not in a museum: its last public appearance was a Paris auction on 29 March 1994, and its present owner is unknown. The uploader to Wikimedia Commons credited it to 'Jan van Kessel III', a mix-up of the family's many Jans that the RKD record corrects.

title: Concert of Cats
collection: Private collection (sold Artcurial, Paris, 23 March 2022, lot 72)
description: A dozen cats crowd around an open songbook, mouths wide, and the score itself is the joke: the notes on the right-hand page are tiny mice, with a whole mouse drawn below them. A grey cat in spectacles bellows at right, another blows a brass trombone at the back, and a black cat lurks in the shadow at lower left. A recorder, a violin and a lute lie abandoned on the floor. It is all painted in oil on a copper plate about the size of a postcard, 13.5 by 16.5 centimetres, made to be held and peered at, and the smooth copper lets every whisker stay sharp.
context: Concerts of cats were a favourite Flemish joke, often teamed with owls or monkeys, and Jan van Kessel the Elder (1626–1679), of the Antwerp Brueghel dynasty, specialised in small animal pictures on copper for collectors. This one is dated to about 1650 to 1660 and is not in a museum: it was sold at Artcurial in Paris on 23 March 2022 (lot 72). The notes on the open songbook are tiny mice, with a whole mouse drawn below the staves, and the heading above the score reads Canona, so even the music is a pun on the singers.
feline_symbolism: A cat choir is a stock image of discord and noise, a parody of human music-making.

title: The Cat of Kazan (Kot Kazanskiy)
collection: Holding impression not identified (reproduced from D. A. Rovinsky, Russkie narodnye kartinki, 1900)
description: A big striped cat sits bolt upright and stares straight out with round green eyes, whiskers fanned wide like a moustache, posed like a dignitary in a state portrait. The caption block at top left gives him his titles: 'Cat of Kazan, mind of Astrakhan, reason of Siberia', a mock string of honours in the manner of a tsar's style. His coat is dense black hatching that coils into a spiral on the haunch, and flowers and a little bird fill the space around him. It is a cheap popular print, made to be pinned to a cottage wall and laughed at.
context: Cheaply printed broadsheets hawked at Moscow markets and pinned to peasant cottage walls carried this single portrait, an eighteenth-century lubok spin-off of the older Mice Are Burying the Cat, and both name the cat 'Alabrys'. The historian S. F. Faizov reads Kazan, Astrakhan and Siberia as the khanates Muscovy conquered in the sixteenth century, and the cat as a composite figure of a Tatar ruler or of Peter the Great. The print is best known today through D. A. Rovinsky's catalogue Russian Folk Pictures (1900). Fun fact: Faizov points to the spiral on the cat's coat, absent from earlier versions, as a coiled serpent, hinting at the Old Believers' view of Peter as the Antichrist.
artist_dates: active mid-18th century
location: State Historical Museum / Pushkin Museum, Moscow
feline_symbolism: Scholars read the cat as a mock ruler, either a conquered Tatar khan or Peter the Great, with titles that parody the tsar's own.

title: The Mice are Burying the Cat
artist_dates: active 18th century
collection: Holding impression not identified (versions in Russian museum collections; image reproduced on Wikimedia Commons)
description: Flat on his back on a sledge, the cat has a broad, almost human face turned up and paws bound across his belly, while a long procession of mice hauls him off to the graveyard. Each mouse has its own job and its own joking caption: musicians, mourners, drink-bearers, a mouse urging the team on. They march in numbered rows above and below the bier, coloured in quick dabs of red and brown. In some versions a mouse still sits in the dead cat's mouth.
context: The earliest surviving versions are woodcuts usually placed at the end of the seventeenth century; eighteenth-century editions were mostly engraved on copper and nineteenth-century ones lithographed. Nineteenth-century scholars, Rovinsky and Stasov among them, read it as an Old Believer satire on Peter the Great's funeral, while M. A. Alekseeva later argued that this was anachronistic for the early versions, which she saw as carnival parody. Fun fact: Stasov called it 'capital in the history of Russian popular development', high praise for a joke about mice.

feline_symbolism: Long read as a satire on a dead tyrant, usually Peter the Great, although recent scholars prefer to see a carnival parody in which the oppressor is mocked by the oppressed.

title: Nude Woman with a Cat (Akt kobiety z kotem)
artist_dates: Polish, Warsaw 1885–1939 Jeziory
location: Private collection (catalogued in Katalog dzieł malarskich)
description: A small white cat with dark patches rolls on its back in the lower left corner, legs in the air, while a female nude lies stretched diagonally across a dark ground with her back to us and her head turned away at upper right. Oil on canvas, from around 1912. This is early Witkacy, before the Formism and the commercial pastel portraits that made him famous, and before he settled on annotating works with codes. Around 1911–12 he was in a turbulent affair with the actress Irena Solska. The painting is catalogued as I 0175 in the catalogue of his paintings. Fun fact: in 1914, after the suicide of his fiancée Jadwiga Janczewska, he joined Bronisław Malinowski's expedition towards New Guinea.

title: Two Kittens in a Basket with a Blue Cloth
description: Two kittens rest their front paws on the edge of a basket covered with a blue cloth: a tortoiseshell-and-white one gazes up and away, and a ginger-and-white one stares straight at us with wide blue eyes. The canvas is 19 × 27 cm, signed upper right. The basket is the classic Adam stage: it frames the kittens and keeps them more or less in one place. A weathered wooden fence and wisps of hay fill the background, and the blue cloth is the colour accent, cool against warm browns and white fur.
context: Sándor Wagner and Johann Leonhard Raab taught Adam alongside Wilhelm von Diez at the Munich Academy, where he became a professor in 1892. Fun fact: a photograph survives of Adam at work in his studio painting a cat.

title: Reclining Kitten (Liegendes Kätzchen)
description: A kitten lies stretched along a slanting ridge, head drooped over one front paw and eyes nearly shut, with a dark stump jutting up beneath it. The sheet is just 12.5 × 20 cm, painted in watercolour, postcard size: in 1913 Marc was making small painted cards and sheets alongside his big canvases, and they let him work fast. The kitten is built from a few thin washes and pencil-like contour, and the bare paper does much of the drawing. Up top, a crescent moon and a scatter of stars turn the nap into a night scene.
context: Else Lasker-Schüler, the poet Marc met in December 1912, received 28 hand-painted postcards from him, and 1913 was also the year he married Maria Franck in Munich on 3 June and painted the large Fate of the Animals. This small watercolour is known from the art market, recorded by Artnet; there is no museum record. Fun fact: older records called it an oil on cardboard with a catalogue-raisonné number, but the only sourced data describe a watercolour about the size of a postcard.

title: Girl with a Cat (Dziewczynka z kotem)
description: A ginger-and-white cat sits in a girl's arms at the bottom of the sheet, ears up and eyes narrowed to amber slits, looking far less impressed than she does. She wears a white headscarf and looks straight out at us, with red geraniums in a pot by the window behind her. The pastel is 50 × 40 cm, a standard upright portrait sheet, signed lower right "LŁempicka". title: Lady with Panther (Dame à la panthère)
description: A black panther lies along the base of the picture at the feet of a standing woman, head raised, tail curling up at the left, and the joke is that the cat is nearly as well accessorised as she is: it wears a blue jewelled collar. She stretches long ropes of pearls between her hands, in a pale Poiret-style gown spotted in brown with a checked hem. Barbier works in watercolour with crisp outlines and flat colour, the fashion-plate manner of the Gazette du Bon Ton, and frames the pair between two red columns. '1914 George Barbier' sits lower right and 'CARTIER Copyright' at the foot.
context: Invitations are rarely this well dressed. Louis Cartier commissioned Barbier in 1914 for a watercolour to serve as the invitation to an exhibition at the firm's boutique in the rue de la Paix, according to several accounts, and it is usually counted as the panther's debut in Cartier imagery, in a year that also saw the first panther-spot wristwatch. The sources are brand histories and magazine pieces rather than the Cartier archive, and they disagree on whether the commission dates to 1913 or 1914. Barbier, a friend of Louis Cartier, is said to have designed over a hundred jewellery pieces for him.
submovement: Parisian fashion illustration (Gazette du Bon Ton circle)
feline_symbolism: Cartier's own story ties the panther to Jeanne Toussaint's independence, and the motif became a house emblem of untamed luxury.

title: Cat on a Flowering Summer Meadow (Katt i blommande sommaräng)
description: A tabby cat peers out of a summer meadow, only its head and a bit of striped shoulder showing, eyes half closed against the light, a little right of centre on a canvas 75.5 × 91 cm. The meadow takes up most of the room: blue-green grass in thick, choppy strokes, yellow flowers scattered everywhere, white daisies piled in the top right corner. Stripes and grass are close cousins, and the tabby pattern lets the animal half dissolve into its surroundings, a hunter's camouflage set inside a quiet summer day. Liljefors signs and dates it lower left.

The tabby pattern is a good match for the stripes of grass and shade, and the cat is easy to miss at first glance.

title: Girl with a Cat: The Fairy (Dziewczyna z kotem: Wróżka)
description: Perched on the young woman's shoulder, a black cat stands with its back arched against the red wall behind, yellow eyes glinting and one front leg dangling down over her bare collarbone. It is clearly the one in charge of the seating plan. She, the "Wróżka" of the title, leans her head sideways under a gold-and-peacock turban and gives us a sly half-smile. Wasilkowski paints in oil on a modest canvas, 47.5 × 57 cm, wider than tall, signed "Kaz. Wł. Wasilkowski" lower right. Wróżka can mean fortune-teller or fairy, and a black cat at the ear suits either trade.
context: Paris, 1900, is where Wasilkowski's Żądze won a gold medal at the Exposition. Kazimierz Władysław Wasilkowski (c. 1861–1934) trained in Warsaw under Wojciech Gerson, in Kraków, and from 1884 to 1890 at the St Petersburg Academy, then settled in Warsaw with his wife, the painter Maria Nostitz-Wasilkowska. He specialised in portraits and sensual female figures drawn from the Bible, folklore and history; one 1935 reviewer said the stated idea was often a pretext for showing the female form in new variations. This canvas, dated around 1920, is in private hands and is known from a Polswiss Art auction listing.

title: Story of a Sick Kitten (Historia chorego kotka)
artist_dates: Polish, Warsaw 1885–1939 Jeziory
description: A sick kitten stands on a little round table at the bottom of the sheet, tail out, far too small for the crowd around it. Baron von Hahn, "a well-known hygienist" according to the pencilled caption, looms over it with a long white beard and reaches down to stroke it; his wife Eufemja hovers, very worried; Dr Rozalja Herzberg has had herself washed and prescribed a sedative draught. At left a pessimist, Robert Holt, disagrees with everyone; at right Konstancja Przepiórkowska stays indifferent. Pencil on a sheet barely 13 by 15 cm, signed and dated lower left, with the cast list written into the picture.
context: Deadpan captions and a crowd of named onlookers turn one poorly kitten into a pencil sitcom. Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz (Witkacy, 1885–1939) is best known for commissioned pastel portraits, but he also filled small sheets with invented characters. This one is signed "Witkacy / 1928 I", January 1928, and is catalogued as I 753 in the catalogue raisonné of his pictorial works. It is in a private collection and reached Wikimedia Commons by way of witkacologia.eu, a site devoted to anecdotes about the artist. The joke is the over-staffing: one kitten, five named grown-ups, among them a hygienist, a doctor and a professional pessimist.

title: Chat (Lidded Box with Cat Head)
artist_dates: French, Ay 1860–1945 Paris
medium: Pressed molded glass, satin-finished and polished
description: From the lid of a small, square pressed-glass box, a cat's face looks up: a relief head with long radiating whiskers, slit pupils and a fixed, level gaze. Lalique plays two finishes against each other, satin-frosted glass for the cat and clear polished glass around it, so the face appears to float above the surface. In this example the recesses of the fur hold a warm brownish tone, which makes the ears and whisker pads read almost like an engraving. The box is roughly 10 by 10 by 5 cm and, the dealer says, engraved "R. Lalique" underneath.

Lidded boxes for powder, jewellery or sweets were a staple of Lalique's Art Deco output, made in series from moulds. This example was offered by the dealer Azur Antik of Mandelieu on the Côte d'Azur as an Art Deco period piece, priced at €1,550. The dealer calls it rare, a claim that is hard to test for a moulded production object.

title: Chat Couché (Reclining Cat Statuette)
artist: Lalique France, after a 1932 model by René Lalique
artist_dates: French, Ay 1860–1945 Paris

title: I Fell in Love with a Lovely Kitten
medium: Gouache, watercolor, and graphite on paper
description: Head and chest only, a brown tabby kitten gazes up and sideways with huge yellow eyes and a small round "o" of a mouth, as if caught admiring something. Wain sets it on a sky-blue ground inside a painted red border and lets the caption below do half the work: "I fell in love with a lovely kitten. & that kitten was myself." The line turns a pet portrait into a joke about vanity, the cat as narrator and object of its own affection. Wain often wrote punning captions straight on to his pictures; here the brushed lettering and the signature just above it are part of the composition.
context: Captions were part of the act for Wain (1860–1939), who made his living from cats that behaved like people. This picture is undated, and its whereabouts are not recorded in any source I could open: the Wikimedia Commons file was taken from a social-media account that posts Wain images, and gives only "before 1940". The old link to Bethlem Museum of the Mind and the date of c. 1930–1935 could not be confirmed. What can be said is that the self-regarding caption matches Wain's long habit of putting first-person jokes into a cat's mouth, a habit he kept up through his hospital years at Bethlem and Napsbury.
title_eng: I Fell in Love with a Lovely Kitten

title: Cat and Rock (hanging scroll)
description: Crouched on all fours, a white long-haired cat with black patches over one ear, across the back and down a thick black tail looks straight out at us with pale, wide-set eyes. Xu builds the coat from quick, feathery grey strokes and leaves most of it bare paper. The source scroll is described as ink and colour on paper, narrow and tall at about 100 by 34 cm, titled Cat and Rock. The image here is a cut-out detail of the cat alone, lifted from the full scroll; the rock and the rest of the composition are outside the frame.
context: Galloping horses are what Xu Beihong (1895–1953) is best known for, but cats recur in his ink paintings of the 1930s and 1940s. He had studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris from 1919 and spent his career fusing Western observation with Chinese brushwork. This scroll, catalogued on Commons as Cat and Rock (猫石图轴), was extracted from a Palace Museum PDF, but I could not find a Palace Museum collection record, and the date is unknown. Fun fact: from 1939 to 1941 Xu toured Singapore, Malaya and India selling his paintings to raise war-relief funds for China and met Tagore and Gandhi, but nothing ties this scroll to that trip.

title: Figaro (frame from the Pinocchio trailer, 1940)
artist: Walt Disney Productions (Animation by Eric Larson)
description: Figaro, Geppetto's black-and-white kitten, is fast asleep in this single frame from the 1940 theatrical trailer for Pinocchio, about a minute in. He wears a floppy red nightcap, eyes shut in two contented curves, white paws resting on a pale blue blanket, with a purple-and-tan patchwork quilt pulled up below. He is pure 1940 Disney character design: a round head and a body built to squash and stretch. The frame is a film still, not a drawing, so what survives is the finished, inked-and-painted cel as photographed by the studio camera, night-blue shadows and all.
context: Figaro is not in Collodi's novel. The Disney story team added him, along with Cleo the goldfish, to give Geppetto a household, and Eric Larson did most of his animation; Clarence Nash, better known as Donald Duck, supplied his noises. Pinocchio premiered at the Center Theatre in New York on 7 February 1940 and went on general release on 23 February. Audiences took to the sulky kitten fast enough that the studio put him into several shorts in the 1940s, and later recast him for good as Minnie Mouse's pet. The trailer frame is in the US public domain because the trailer was published without a copyright notice, an accident of 1940 paperwork that the feature itself did not share.

title: Dora Maar with Cat (Dora Maar au chat)
collection: Private collection (sold Sotheby's New York, 3 May 2006, sale N08195, lot 14)
description: A small black cat perches behind Dora Maar on the back of a big wooden armchair, right beside her neck, in what Sotheby's called "both an amusing and menacing attitude". She sits three-quarter length, enthroned, in a hat sprouting coloured feathers, and her face is shown from two angles at once, profile and front folded into one head. Her striped green bodice and red polka-dot skirt fight for attention, and her long painted nails turn into talons on the armrests, so the cat is not the only creature in the picture with claws. Oil on canvas, about 130 by 97 cm, signed lower left.
context: Black cat behind the neck, talons for fingernails: Dora Maar was photographer, painter and poet, and Picasso's lover and main model since the mid-1930s. He painted her in Paris in 1941, early in the German occupation. Sotheby's New York sold the canvas on 3 May 2006 for $95,216,000, nearly double the estimate, to an anonymous bidder reported to be Bidzina Ivanishvili, and it remains in a private collection. Sotheby's catalogue calls the cat's attitude "both an amusing and menacing" one. Picasso is said to have called Maar an "Afghan cat", a remark that rests on Wikipedia's account, not on a primary source seen here.
submovement: Picasso wartime portraiture of Dora Maar
feline_symbolism: Cats paired with women in art have long implied female cunning and sexual aggression, and Picasso's "Afghan cat" nickname for Maar makes the black cat read as her double.
image_credit: © Succession Picasso. Image: Sotheby's, Impressionist & Modern Art Evening Sale N08195 (New York, 2006), lot 14. Shown with credit for identification; the image loads from Sotheby's and is not stored on this site.

title: Simon the Cat, Mascot of HMS Amethyst
title_original: Able Seacat Simon of HMS Amethyst
description: Simon, a small black-and-white cat, poses with three sailors aboard HMS Amethyst in this plain gelatin silver print by an unnamed photographer. It is the kind of informal ship's snapshot that nobody expected a museum to want, and the Imperial War Museum now files it under the cat's own name. The men are the supporting cast here. Note the credit line, the PDSA, the animal charity that gave Simon his medal and kept the pictures that made him famous.
context: Hong Kong docks, March 1948: a 17-year-old seaman, George Hickinbottom, found a stray there and smuggled him aboard HMS Amethyst. In April 1949, during the Yangtze Incident, a shell tore through the captain's cabin; Simon was treated for burns and shrapnel and went back to killing rats. He received the PDSA Dickin Medal in August 1949 and remains the only cat to hold it. He died in quarantine in Surrey on 28 November 1949 and is buried in the PDSA cemetery at Ilford. The print is credited to the PDSA and recorded at IWM North as HU 43656, according to Luminous-Lint. One of his kills was reportedly a rat the crew called 'Mao Tse-tung'.

title: The Mediterranean Cat (Le Chat de la Méditerranée)
license: © Estate of Balthus, all rights reserved
description: Seated at a laid table on a terrace, a cat-headed man in a striped jumper has a napkin tied at his neck, knife and fork at the ready, a wine glass and bottle to hand. Behind him a rainbow rises from the sea and fish leap out of it towards his plate, where a fat one already lies. A lobster waits on a crate at the front, and a woman waves from a rowing boat on the left. It is a big oil, about 127 by 185 cm, in flat, sign-like colour that reads from across a room. The cat is Balthus himself, eyes shut and mouth curled in a grin.
context: A restaurant job lies behind this one: the title points to La Méditerranée, the seafood restaurant opened in 1942 opposite the Théâtre de l'Odéon in Paris, where Balthus is reported to have made the picture in 1949, though the sources opened here do not spell out the commission. He had cast himself as a cat before, in The King of Cats (1935), and as a boy made the forty ink drawings of a stray named Mitsou, published in 1921 with a preface by Rilke. The canvas is in a private collection, and an oil study for it (1949) was later sold at Sotheby's.
feline_symbolism: The cat is the artist's alter ego, a role Balthus gave cats from Mitsou onward.

title: Interior with a Lady and a Cat
collection: Private collection (sold Sotheby's London, The Scandinavian Sale, 2007, lot 415)
description: A black-and-white cat lies stretched out on the bare floorboards by an open doorway, a small dark shape that is easy to miss on first look. The woman, in a long white dress, stands with her back to us at a sunlit window. This is the Danish interior Holsøe painted over and over: pale panelled walls, a gilt console with a vase and a tall mirror, and a second room glimpsed through the door with a rush-seated chair. The panel is 45.5 × 50 cm, almost square, and signed 'C. Holsöe' at lower left. The cat anchors a room that is otherwise all air and reflection.

The condition note mentions a small area of retouching on the floor near the door, which is where the cat lies. Carl Holsøe (1863–1935) painted such hushed Copenhagen interiors for decades, so the lot gives no year and the panel can only be placed within his career.

title: Flowers and Cats (Fleurs et chats)
description: The bottom of this flower still life belongs to two cats: a brown tabby asleep on a red table, head tucked down, and a grey cat peering out beside a basket tied with a red ribbon, a white ball of yarn at the right edge. Above, a huge bank of red and pink geraniums spills from a big decorated bowl on a pedestal, which is rarer than it sounds: Renoir usually kept his cats on people's laps. The canvas is 92.7 × 73.7 cm and signed at lower right, and petals and fur are made with the same soft, feathery strokes, so the animals read as part of the arrangement.
context: A checkered floor and a fiery red wall frame the geraniums, and the painting is better known in English as Geraniums and Cats. It is in a private collection, so there is no museum record; Wikimedia Commons, WikiArt and Artchive all list it as an 1881 oil on canvas, 73.7 × 92.7 cm, and the Commons file is scanned from a Taschen book on Renoir. Fun fact: the two titles, Fleurs et chats and Geraniums and Cats, put the flowers first, but the cats are the only living things in the picture.

title: The Butterfly
description: A fluffy tabby kitten sits with its back to us on a wooden ledge, tail hanging over the edge, head tipped up at a dark butterfly that has landed in a spray of pink-and-white apple blossom. The blossom rises from a blue-and-white vase painted with a bird on a branch, which raises the stakes nicely: one kitten, one butterfly, one breakable object. Dolph painted it in oil on an upright canvas, 71 by 41 cm, and the tall format lets the blossom climb while the kitten stays put, for now. The picture is known as 'The Butterfly', and it is signed at lower left.
context: Apprenticed to a carriage painter in Columbus at fourteen, Dolph was painting portraits in Cleveland and Detroit by 1855, moved to New York in 1864, studied in Antwerp from 1870 to 1873 and afterwards specialised in pets. The Butterfly is known only through the Athenaeum database, which dates it to about 1870, and its present owner is unrecorded. He lived in the Sherwood Studio Building at 57th Street and Sixth Avenue, which Wikipedia calls the first apartment building in New York made specifically for artists.

title: Apotheosis of the Cats of Montmartre (L'Apothéose des chats à Montmartre)
submovement: Montmartre cabaret decoration (Le Chat Noir circle)
description: A horde of cats pours over the rooftops of Paris under a full moon, and at the very top of the heap one black cat sits silhouetted against the yellow disc like a king on a throne. Numéro describes the felines as invading the roofs, perhaps on their way to besiege the whole city. The canvas is huge, three metres wide and more than one and a half high, so the cats work as a frieze of silhouettes and attitudes: gingers and tabbies scrambling over a chimney at left, a black cat on the gutter, a tangle of orange cats at right. Windmills crown the hill in the distance.
context: Hanging in the downstairs room of Rodolphe Salis's Chat Noir cabaret, according to Numéro, this huge canvas shows a horde of cats that seems to have taken over the roofs of Paris before, perhaps, besieging the whole city. It belongs to the Geneva Petit Palais collection (the Numéro credit reads Association des Amis du Petit Palais, Genève), and it was among the cat paintings in the centenary exhibition of Steinlen at the Musée de Montmartre in 2023–24. Fun fact: the date is contested. Wikimedia and coverage of the exhibition give c. 1885, while Numéro prints 1905, awkward beside its own story of the canvas hanging in the cabaret, since Steinlen's contributions to the Chat Noir paper ran 1884–1895.
title_eng: Apotheosis of the Cats of Montmartre
feline_symbolism: Cats were the cabaret's emblem, named after an old tomcat said to have moved in during building work, so an apotheosis of cats is also an apotheosis of the house.
image_credit: Théophile Steinlen · LeTemps.ch [1]
_audit_notes: Painting is real and appears in the 2023–24 Musée de Montmartre Steinlen exhibition per Numéro (read: credits Studio Monique Bernaz, Genève; dates it 1905; says it hung in the lower room of the Chat Noir). No institutional record page was found (source_url is a Commons page): FLAG, need a Geneva Petit Palais/Musée de Montmartre record. Dimensions 164.5 x 300 and 'Nº 0155' unconfirmed (inv blanked). Image 3413x1920 clear, hordes of cats visible, description accurate (moon, black cat atop the heap, windmills at right). Date c. 1885 vs 1905 unresolved; era 19th century only holds if 1885. Dropped the '630 works' claim. Opener of context (artist name) replaced. Description kept.
reason: Petit Palais Geneva is the private Modern Art Foundation; no online institution record. Queries: 'Steinlen Apotheose des chats Musee d art et d histoire Geneve OR Petit Palais inventaire'; 'Steinlen Apotheose des chats Petit Palais Geneve ferme collection musee accessible'; lane notes (Numero). Only press/Commons.

title: A New Arrival
description: A tricolour cat laps milk from a shallow green-rimmed bowl that a girl holds on her lap, its white muzzle dipped and eyes half closed. She looks down at it in a pale blue pinafore, and behind her a long-case clock, a jug, a teacup and a glass of daffodils fill a plain grey room. The 'new arrival' is being welcomed with food. The canvas is small, 46 × 36 cm, signed and dated 'Walter Osborne 85' at lower left. The treatment is unsentimental: Osborne painted children and their pets with a realist's eye and a gentle mood rather than with the syrup of much Victorian genre painting.
context: Christie's catalogue note reads the room as a modest parlour and the girl's ragged clothes as those of a kitchen maid or farm girl, feeding a tortoiseshell cat from a saucer of milk. Osborne had studied in Antwerp, where he won the Taylor Prize in 1881 and 1882, painted in Brittany from 1883, then worked in England and Ireland, and was elected to the Royal Hibernian Academy in 1886. Fun fact: his father, William Osborne, was an accomplished animal painter, and Walter noticed there was a market for pictures of pets. The picture last surfaced at Christie's in London; today's owner is unrecorded.

title: Pierrot and the Cat (Pierrot et le chat)
description: Hugged upright against a small child's chest, a large black cat stretches to full length, hind paws just reaching the floor and tail curling up at the bottom right, its yellow eyes glinting. The child is dressed as Pierrot, in a white ruffled collar and baggy white suit with a black skullcap, and looks off to the left rather than at the cat. Black against white makes the cat as visible as it could be, and the dark brown ground sets both figures off. The cat has the long-suffering look of an animal that has been carried before. The signature, 'Steinlen', sits at the lower right.
context: Wikimedia Commons records this picture as Steinlen's Pierrot and the cat, 1889, inventory number 14383, attributed to the Musée du Petit Palais in Geneva, the private museum built around the collection of Oscar Ghez. The image circulates through WikiArt under a file name that calls it a private collection instead, so its present owner is not settled. Fun fact: Pierrot, the sad white clown of the Paris stage, was a favourite Montmartre figure, and Steinlen put one into the arms of a toddler, with a cat as the hostage.

title: Little Girl with a Grey Cat (Jeune fille au chat)
description: A grey cat lies across a girl's lap at the lower right, green eyes watching, its head just under her arm, while she leans back against a pink cushion and looks straight out at us. She wears a white ruffled dress and a pearl necklace, her fair hair pinned up. This is La jeune fille au chat, which Morisot painted in the summer of 1892, and the cat is built from the same quick blue-grey strokes as the shadows of the dress, so it almost dissolves into her.
context: Christie's, which sold the canvas in London, names the model as Jeanne Fourmanoir and notes that Morisot exhibited in seven of the eight Impressionist shows, missing one only through illness. It also floats an idea: the languid cat might be a nod to Edouard Manet's Olympia, painted by her brother-in-law. Fun fact: the picture was in the posthumous Morisot retrospective at Durand-Ruel in 1896, a year after her death. The canvas is in a private collection, and no museum record exists.
title_eng: Little Girl with a Grey Cat

title: Sleeping Woman with Cat (Śpiąca kobieta z kotem)
description: At the lower right, a black cat arches its back and lifts its tail, one yellow eye glinting as it brushes against the folds of a sleeping woman's skirt. She lies curled on a sofa of acid green, red hair spread over the cushion, hands folded under her cheek, her black dress a single heavy mass. The canvas is a full metre wide (66 × 100 cm), signed 'W. Ślewiński' at top left. His habits, learned from Gauguin, are all here: forms laid down in flat areas, edges closed with contour, earthy darks lifted by one loud green. The cat is the smallest flat shape, and the only one awake.
context: Russian tax collectors are the reason this Polish painter turned up in Paris. Władysław Ślewiński inherited his family's properties in 1886, was ruined within two years and fled in 1888, hounded by the tax men, and only then decided on painting as a career. He studied at the Académie Colarossi and the Académie Julian from 1888 to 1890, befriended Gauguin in 1889 and spent most of his time at Le Pouldu in Brittany with the Pont-Aven circle. He exhibited at the Salon des Indépendants in 1895 and 1896, the year of this picture. Fun fact: the work is known today through an auction sale; the photograph on Wikimedia comes from the Polish auction house Rempex.

title: Kiribi, portrait de chatte (brooch)
description: Kiribi was a she-cat, and this small silver plaquette is her portrait, made to be worn as a brooch. Her name is cut in tall letters at upper left, with '1898' and 'SYLLA EUSTACHE' at lower right. Low relief is a medallist's habit, and the cat gets the treatment usually kept for a human sitter. The brooch is published in the Tadema Gallery's 2021 jewellery book (p. 68); its location is unknown. In 1919 the magazine La Mode commissioned him to design fantasy jewellery for its subscribers.

title: Sleeping Kitten (Śpiący kotek)
artist_dates: Polish, Radom 1854–1929 Kraków
description: Chin flat on a cushion, a kitten sleeps, ears soft, a few quick strokes for the closed eyes. The great painter of Polish Symbolist allegory here does something modest: he watches an animal that is not going anywhere and gets it down. On the back is a pencil sketch of a hunter, and a pencil '103' runs up the lower left edge.

It has passed through the Polish art market and is recorded on the Artinfo.pl database. Fun fact: the hunter sketch on the verso means the sheet carries two of Malczewski's subjects at once, a quiet cat on one side and a man with a gun on the other.

title: Sara Holding a Cat (Sara tenant un chat)
description: A ginger cat is hugged against a little girl's chest, and it stares out at us with round dark eyes while she gazes down at it with her lids lowered. She is strawberry-blonde, seen at half length in a white dress with pink sleeves and a pink ribbon bow in her hair, against a loosely brushed green ground. Cassatt puts the cat's orange coat right next to her hair and pink arms, so the warm colours almost run together and the cat has to be found by its shape. It is a portrait of a child, but the cat gets almost as much of the picture. Signed top right.
context: Nobody commissioned this child, as the Christie's catalogue note stresses: Cassatt's earlier children were commissions or her nieces and nephews, but the single-child series of 1907–08 'seems to have had no such motivation'. Born in Pittsburgh and settled in France, she had changed her style after a 1901 trip to Italy and Spain with the collectors Louisine and Harry Havemeyer, and this is a product of that late phase. The canvas is signed at upper right and sold at Christie's New York in 2012. It is in a private collection, so no museum record exists. Fun fact: the same note calls it 'a touching portrayal of a young girl's tender bond with her feline companion'.

title: Cats on a Red Cloth (Katzen auf rotem Tuch)
description: Sleeping in one heap, a black-and-white cat curls at lower left with its head tucked out of sight, while an orange-and-white cat drapes over the back of it, chin on its paws, one foreleg stretched across its sleeping partner. Oil on canvas, about 50.5 by 60.5 cm. The red cloth is the event, a hot slab of colour wedged under the pair and dragged on in long stripes, while the floor around them churns in yellow straw strokes. The cats read as pattern as much as animals, Marc moving toward the unmixed colour of his next two years. Signed "Marc" lower right.
context: Winter 1910–11 turned Marc's palette to bright primaries, and this canvas, painted in 1909–10, stands just before that change. He had gone to Paris in 1903 and 1907 and felt a strong affinity with Van Gogh, and in 2007 this canvas was shown as plate 31 in the catalogue Van Gogh and Expressionism. PubHist places it in the Deutsche Bank art collection and lists it as Hoberg/Jansen 109. Later, red would become a loaded colour for Marc, standing for violence; here it is still just a cloth.

title: Girl with Cat I (Mädchen mit Katze I)
description: A dark cat arches in the girl's arms, back curved into a crescent and head turned up toward her, while she looks down at it with half-closed eyes and a small smile, one hand cupped over its body. The two lock together into one block on a nearly square canvas, 71 × 67.5 cm, the format Marc liked for exactly this. A pale shawl wraps the group like a frame. This is the first of two versions; Marc came back to the subject in 1912 with Girl with Cat II, almost the same size. Already the cat is a simple dark silhouette rather than fur and whiskers.
context: Blue the male principle, yellow the female, red matter to be overcome: Franz Marc set out this colour code in a letter to August Macke of 12 December 1910, the winter he and Maria Franck had moved to Sindelsdorf in Upper Bavaria and he was painting the first version of this picture (1910/11). Within a year he and Kandinsky had founded Der Blaue Reiter. The canvas is in a private collection. Fun fact: Marc came back to the subject in 1912 with Girl with Cat II, almost the same size, in which the cat is even simpler.

title: Cat and Dog (Kot i piesek)
artist_dates: Polish, active late 19th – early 20th century
description: A grey-and-white cat curls up with its pointed ears tucked against a much bigger dark sleeper, the two bodies fitted together into a single low oval on a muddy ochre ground. Oil on card was the cheap, quick support of the period, good for studies and small saleable pictures, and the brushwork stays visible here, thick and creamy in the white fur, scrubbed thin in the background.
