title: Kinderbild (Cat behind a Tree)
artist_dates: German, Munich 1880–1916 Braquis (Verdun)
collection: Private collection (restituted to the heirs of Alfred and Thekla Hess 2009; sold Christie's London, 24 June 2014)
description: An orange cat sleeps curled around the back of a blue tree trunk, its white-muzzled face peeking out on the left, eyes shut, and its round haunch and tail bulging out on the right, as if the tree were a screen it chose on purpose. Around it the landscape breaks into flat zones of green, yellow and blue. Nothing is shaded in the academic way; colour does the modelling and the cat is mostly a warm shape held by a cool one. It is 70.2 × 50 cm, oil on canvas, and its German title, Kinderbild, marks it as a picture with children in mind.
context: Restitution gave this picture a second life. Marc painted it in 1910–11 in Sindelsdorf; it was shown at the Neue Künstlervereinigung München in March 1911, and later belonged to Alfred and Thekla Hess of Erfurt, Jewish collectors forced to sell under Nazi persecution. It passed through the Berlin dealers Nierendorf and Thannhauser around 1935 and was acquired in 1936 by Günther Wagner of the Pelikan company. From 1950 it hung on loan in Hanover, later at the Sprengel Museum. Fun fact: in 2009 it was restituted to the Hess heirs, and in June 2014 it sold at Christie's London for £6,242,500.

title: Cats, Red and White (Katzen, rot und weiß)
artist_dates: German, Munich 1880–1916 Braquis (Verdun)
description: Pressed together, a white cat and a red cat share one silhouette: the white one faces us with narrow amber eyes and a few quick black whiskers, the red one turned away so we see only its back, its ear and a long tail sweeping down over a dark blue shape at the bottom. Their heads overlap so closely they almost merge. The canvas is upright, 52 × 35 cm, small and tall, like a door left ajar. The red is not a ginger coat; it is Marc's red, the colour he tied to matter and weight. The contrast between the two animals, one open and one turned away, is the whole subject.
context: The Blaue Reiter almanac appeared in the spring of 1912, the year Marc painted this in Sindelsdorf. The colour code he had set out in a letter to August Macke in December 1910, blue male, yellow female, red the matter the other two must overcome, explains the red cat as much as any ginger coat does. The painting is in a private collection. Fun fact: it is not Marc's "The White Cat" of 1912, which is in Halle and shows a white tomcat on a yellow cushion, so the two are easily confused.
feline_symbolism: Marc gave colours fixed meanings: red stood for matter, heavy and earthbound, which makes the red cat a deliberate counterweight to the white one.

title: Cat and Her Kittens in a Painter's Studio (Dans l'atelier)
description: A mother cat and her kittens have the run of a painter's studio, the room where Ronner-Knip spent her working life watching exactly these animals. Her cats are always built from close, directional strokes that follow the lie of the fur, with eyes given a glassy highlight, and the setting is there to give them things to climb, hide behind and knock over. The joke is at the artist's own expense: in this studio the models are in charge, and the painter is absent.
context: A house in Ixelles with a large garden held the models: in her later years Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) kept hunting dogs, cats and a parrot there, born in Amsterdam but based in Brussels from 1850. After 1870 she painted her most famous works, long-haired and often playful cats in bourgeois settings. The image comes from the Ede dealer Simonis & Buunk, whose catalogue lists a 54.5 × 72 cm oil on panel titled 'Cat and her kittens in a painter's studio', catalogued there as dated 1878; its owner is a private collector. Fun fact: she was the first woman admitted as an active member of the Amsterdam artists' society Arti et Amicitiae.

title: A Monster
description: Upper right, a tabby cat peeks over the back of a wicker chair, eyes wide, front paws hooked on the rim, keeping well clear of the action. The 'monster' is the little girl herself: she crawls out from under a draped table wearing a whole tiger skin, its head pulled over her curls as a hood, while a pug squares up to her on the carpet. Alphabet blocks lie scattered at the bottom edge. Barber's speciality was fur of every kind, and here he gets three textures in one picture: the child's hair, the coarse striped pelt and the pets' coats.
context: Great Yarmouth, on the Norfolk coast, was where Charles Burton Barber (1845–1894) was born; he studied at the Royal Academy from the age of eighteen, won a silver medal for drawing in 1864 and exhibited there from 1866 to 1893. He specialised in sentimental pictures of children and their pets, took commissions from Queen Victoria and the Prince of Wales, and saw many works sold as photogravures. A Monster is dated 1877, and Commons records no present location. Fun fact: his last commission, in 1894, was to paint the Queen with her grandchildren in her pony carriage, and he died in London soon afterwards.

title: Studies of an Awakening Kitten
medium: Oil on paper laid down on panel
collection: Unknown (reproduced in Simonis & Buunk catalogue 'Harmonie en Contrast')
description: One sheet, three calico kittens, or perhaps one kitten three times: two curled asleep at left, eyes shut and paws tucked, and one at right sitting up wide awake, with round blue eyes and a ginger patch over one of them. The title says studies, plural, and the sheet reads like the moment when a kitten's eyes open before the rest of the body agrees. The warm ground is brushed in loosely around each figure. Ronner-Knip painted in oil on paper, later laid on panel, 27.1 by 36.1 cm, and marked it twice at lower right: with the initials 'HR' and the full signature 'Henriette Ronner'.
context: Oil sketches on paper were her working tools: late in life she kept live models, watched them, then folded paper figures into the poses she wanted. Trained by her father Joseph August Knip, she exhibited in Amsterdam from 1838, became the first woman active member of Arti et Amicitiae, moved to Brussels in 1850 and turned to cats after 1870. The sheet is published in Harmonie en Contrast, a catalogue of the Dutch dealers Simonis & Buunk in Ede, which is the source of the reproduction. Its present owner is not recorded.

title: The Maine Coon
description: A long-haired tabby with a white bib sits square to us on a pale blue cloth, green eyes fixed just past the viewer, its huge tail swept round in front of its feet. It fills an upright panel 40.5 by 32 cm, painted in oil. The coat is the subject: a long-haired cat lets a painter show off, and the fur here is dragged on in short, broken strokes of brown, black and grey over a mottled buff ground. The auction title calls the sitter a Maine Coon, but that is a saleroom label, not Ronner-Knip's. The inscription at upper left, 'Henriette Ronner./94', fixes the year as 1894.
context: By 1894 Ronner-Knip (1821–1909) had spent more than four decades in Brussels and two in cats; her best-known pictures are of long-haired cats in comfortable interiors, and she received the Order of Leopold in 1887. This panel came through the Amsterdam dealer Kunsthandel M. Wolff and was offered as lot 252 at Christie's sale 17295 of nineteenth-century European and Orientalist art in December 2019. Fun fact: Wikimedia Commons now files the picture under 'History of Maine Coon cats', so a painting made in Brussels, titled by an auction house, has been drafted into an American breed's family album.

title: Kittens with a Basket of Lobsters (Kätzchen)
description: Flat on its back, a tabby-and-white kitten lies on a crumpled cloth, all four paws up and mouth wide open, squaring off against a lobster whose claw dangles over the edge of a tipped wicker basket. A second kitten peers over the basket rim at upper right, hissing too, and a label with a red seal is tucked into the lid. Julius Adam painted the encounter in watercolour and gouache on paper, a small upright sheet of 26.5 by 19 cm, and signed it 'Jul. Adam.' at upper right. Soft fur against hard shell is the whole gag, and gouache lets him lay opaque highlights on both.
context: Four generations of Adams painted in Munich, and this one began in his father's photographic studio. At fourteen he set off for Rio de Janeiro as a landscape photographer, then studied at the Munich Academy from 1873, six years of it under Wilhelm von Diez. He set up as a painter in 1882, turned to cats, and became 'Katzen-Adam' and 'Katzenraffael', with a strong market in the United States. Fun fact: in 1887 he signed a dealer contract obliging him to paint only for that dealer's clients for five years. This sheet surfaced through the German auction house Van Ham.

title: Marsh Scene with Cat and Birds
title_eng: Marsh Scene with Cat and Birds
artist_dates: Unknown
submovement: Saite Archaizing Tomb Relief (Marsh Scene after Old Kingdom models)
collection: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland
image_credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of the Hanna Fund, 1949.498 (Open Access, CC0)
description: A thicket of papyrus stalks fills the slab, each topped with a spreading umbel, and the carver has left traces of red, grey and black on them. Two tall birds, a hoopoe and a crane according to Cleveland, perch high up on the right. Down at the bottom left, below the water line, a cat-like hunter arches over a nest of birds with one paw reaching in while the nest's owners flap above it. The break at the left edge cuts off the next scene, where, Cleveland suggests, a mongoose probably attacked another nest.
context: A civet cat, says Cleveland's label, is the nest raider, so that identification is the museum's own, worth keeping in mind beside the cat-like body and tail shown here. It also notes that the scene is "essentially copied from Old Kingdom work", with a few details borrowed from the New Kingdom. That is the signature of the Saite revival, when sculptors of the 7th century BCE deliberately went back to Old Kingdom tomb models. A cat raiding nests in the papyrus thicket belongs to the same marsh-scene tradition as the cat in the Nebamun fowling scene.
feline_symbolism: A marsh hunter among the papyrus, in a scene type meant to show the abundance of the afterlife.
reason: Cleveland's own label says the nest raider is a 'civet cat' (and a mongoose at left): not a felid. Civet cat is a non-felid, so it fails rule 1.

title: Pussy at the Brighton Cat Show
medium: Pen, black ink, and zinc process engraving on newsprint
collection: Newspaper illustration, South Wales Daily News, 21 November 1895
description: Four cat heads crowd one newspaper block, and the biggest, top left, is labelled 'Sam Woodiwiss's Champion Xenophon', a heavyweight brown tabby and one of the most decorated show cats of the decade. Around him sit a pale cat at top right, a Persian tabby at lower left and, at lower right, a Persian labelled 'Shazada'. The printed caption reads 'The Premier Cats of England (By Louis Wain)'. It ran in the South Wales Daily News on 21 November 1895. Wain drew for the press in pen and ink, so everything is line and hatching, made to survive cheap newsprint and fast presses.
context: Frances Simpson's The Book of the Cat mourned Champion Xenophon with 'We shall ne'er look on his like again', after the brown tabby had been, in her words, the 'world-renowned champion of champions'. He changed hands several times, among his owners Sam Woodiwiss of East Finchley, named in this drawing's caption, and later Lady Gertrude Decies, who also owned the chinchilla Zaida, his great rival for top honours. Wain, who judged and reported on cat shows, drew the fancy from inside. This clipping ran on 21 November 1895. Fun fact: on the show bench Xenophon was reportedly never beaten in his class.

title: National Cat Show at the Crystal Palace
medium: Pen, black ink, and mechanical engraving on newsprint
collection: Newspaper illustration, Bromley & District Times, 23 October 1896
description: Cats in roundels and cats in a heap: this double-page spread captioned 'The Crystal Palace Cat Show', printed in the Bromley & District Times on 23 October 1896, sets a black-and-white cat, a tabby and a black cat in framed medallions, with a fluffy cat in a large roundel at right and four Siamese crowded together at lower left. A small tabby head near the top carries the label 'Champion Xenophon'. Wain's show drawings are portraits of real, named animals, done in pen line that could be reproduced cheaply, and they reward a magnifier: the set of the ears, a fold of a cheek, a tail that could only belong to one cat.
context: Sydenham, where the Crystal Palace stood, is a short trip from Bromley, which explains why a local weekly wanted a cat-show page of its own. Wain drew the same autumn 1896 event for The Illustrated London News the following day. Fun fact: the champion the page names, Xenophon, was reportedly never beaten in his class during his show career, according to the Cat-o-pedia history project, and on occasion took Best Cat in Show.

title: Jerzual Street in Dinan (with a Cat)
collection: Unknown (impression offered at Nautilus auction, Poland)
description: Look for a small pale shape trotting across the cobbles at lower centre, tail out, the one moving thing in the rue du Jerzual. The Polish title adds '(z kotem)', 'with a cat', as if you are meant to hunt for it. Pankiewicz looks down the steep medieval street in Dinan toward the river Rance, timber-framed houses leaning in on the right, dark doorways under their overhangs, a few figures far down the slope. The needle lines follow beams, cobbles and slate. 'Dinan' is etched at lower right and the sheet signed in pencil below.
context: Born in Lublin in 1866, Józef Pankiewicz trained in Warsaw and St Petersburg and went to Paris in 1889; in 1906 he became a professor at the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts, and later he mentored the 'Kapists'. He spent repeated summers in France and made paintings and etchings of the towns he stayed in. This etching, catalogued on Commons as 'Ulica Jerzual w Dinan (z kotem)' and dated 1906 or 1908, is known from an impression offered at a Polish auction (Nautilus, via artinfo.pl); I found no National Museum in Warsaw record. The odd detail is the title itself: a street view whose only named inhabitant is the cat.

title: A Christmas Ball at Catville
medium: Color relief process on newsprint (Sunday comic section)
collection: Newspaper Sunday supplement (US), via Origins of the Sunday Comics
description: A ballroom crammed with dancing cats: couples pair off across the floor on their hind legs in tailcoats and long gowns, under two holly wreaths tied with red bows. A cat band saws and blows away in the gallery at upper right, beside a sign for ICES, and at lower left one dancer has gone flat on the floor while another sprawls over her. Wain fills the sheet edge to edge, so the eye moves from one grinning face to the next like a guest scanning the room. Made for newspaper printing, the outlines are firm. Nobody in the room seems to notice that they are all cats.
context: Dated 5 December 1909, the page comes from Wain's American years: he went to New York in 1907 on a contract with Hearst Newspapers and returned to England in 1910 after his mother died. The image on Commons comes from the Origins of the Sunday Comics project, which collects early American newspaper comic supplements, so this was almost certainly printed in a Sunday colour section for Christmas. The odd fact: Wain, who had invented the cat Christmas party in the Illustrated London News in 1886, was still selling the same idea, now to American readers, twenty-three years later.

title: Catland: Dragging the Yule Log
collection: Unknown (reproduction found on a blog; original and holder not identified)
description: A gang of Wain's cats hauls a Yule log home through the snow on a rope at lower left, while the rest of Catland has given up work for tobogganing: cats pile onto sledges, tumble off them, wave their paws and go head over heels down the slope. One black cat has landed upside down in a drift. title: Angora Cat Watching a Bird
title_original: Un chat Angola qui guette un oiseau
collection: Private collection (exhibited at the Salon of 1761)
description: A white Angora cat, all plume and ruff, stops mid-stride and stares straight up at a small grey-and-white bird in flight just above its head, wings spread against dark foliage. Bachelier makes the long coat the real subject, building the fur in soft white masses, while the tail rises behind like a feather duster held up in alarm. The pink nose and upturned gaze make the cat's concentration look faintly absurd. The cat takes up most of the canvas, with a clump of green leaves at lower right, and gets the attention a portrait sitter would.

title: A Lady with Her Cat
description: A large white cat with ginger patches on its head and a ginger tail sits on the table at left, head slightly tilted, fixing us with yellow-green eyes. Beside it a young woman in white muslin and a starched ruff rests her arm on a blue shawl and holds a small ring-shaped object, curls pinned up, a little gold earring catching the light. The cat's direct gaze mirrors its owner's composure, as if the two had agreed to pose together, and its tail hangs over the table edge like a bell-pull. The picture is small, 32.4 by 24.5 cm, and signed 'Mle Gerard' at lower left.
context: 'Oil on panel,' said the Christie's catalogue, until a saleroom notice admitted the painting is on canvas, which is why online copies still disagree about its support. Christie's, which offered it as lot 34, calls it a characteristic example of Gérard's mature style, with a cool, silver-toned palette and precise surface detail, and notes that she specialised in wives and mothers, often with children, servants or pets. Fun fact: Gérard was only 'unofficially' apprenticed to her brother-in-law Fragonard, yet by the late 1780s Christie's ranks her among France's leading women artists.

title: Portrait of Marguerite Gérard with Her Cat
collection: Private collection (sold Ader, Hôtel Drouot, Paris, 3 November 2022, lot 28)
description: Peeping over the sitter's shoulder, a fluffy, dark-masked cat presses its round-eyed face against her cheek. This is a portrait of Marguerite Gérard, not by her: a roundel in black chalk, only 17.3 cm across. Her face is fully worked up, frank and faintly amused, while bonnet, kerchief and dress dissolve into loose outline, so the eye travels from her face straight to the cat's. On the original mount, outside this photograph, a four-line verse praises the sitter as formed by Love and the Arts, then grumbles that a cat is an odd companion and she ought to be holding the bird of Venus instead.
context: Three generations of the Pajou family probably kept this roundel, from the painter's son Augustin-Désiré Pajou (1800–1878) via Joseph-Auguste Pajou (1824–1885) to Louise Marie-Saint-Germain, née Pajou (1855–1940). It is no. 117 in P. Nusbaumer's 1997 catalogue of Jacques-Augustin-Catherine Pajou (1766–1828), to whom it is attributed, and is dated to the end of the eighteenth or the start of the nineteenth century. It sold at Ader, Hôtel Drouot, Paris, on 3 November 2022 (lot 28) for €4,864 against an estimate of €3,000–4,000. Fun fact: the verse on the mount scolds Gérard for her pet and offers Venus's dove as the proper accessory, a swap she evidently ignored.

title: Trompe-l'œil with a Cat and a Log through a Canvas
title_original: Trompe-l'œil avec un chat et une bûche de bois à travers une toile
description: A grey, fluffy cat pushes through a rip in a canvas, its face peering out above a sawn log lying across the hole. Everything is painted, the tear included, and we are looking at the back of a picture: bare canvas, wooden stretcher bars and wedged corners. Fish hang from a string on the upper right, and through a second tear at lower right sits a plate with something dark on it. Boilly lays out the props of a kitchen still life, log and fish, then lets the cat break the frame to get at them. At 85 by 96 cm the trick works from across a room.

The two were old friends who once shared lodgings in Paris. Christie's offered it as property of a lady, and its sale-room notice says the canvas was once used as a chimney screen. Fun fact: Boilly's trompe-l'oeil A Collection of Drawings, shown at the Salon of 1800, drew such crowds that a balustrade had to be set up in front of it.

title: A Cat in a Cage
collection: Holding institution not identified (watercolour, c. 1800; reproduced on Wikimedia Commons)
description: Inside a gilded birdcage a tabby cat crouches, body hunched, staring out through the bars, and the margins explain why: mice everywhere. They scurry over the sandy ground, sit up on a broken tree stump, nibble in pairs and peer from holes, a whole town out to enjoy the jailing of the enemy. Mind worked in watercolour, building fur from small strokes of thin colour over a light drawing, and the cage's thin gold bars cut across the cat's striped coat like ruled lines. Crumbling ruins and a blue mountain turn the joke into a landscape.
context: 'That is no cat!' is what Gottfried Mind is said to have told his master Sigmund Freudenberger when he saw a cat in one of the master's sketches; challenged to do better, he drew one so good that Freudenberger let him finish the figure and began copying his pupil's work. Mind was born in Bern in 1768 and apprenticed to Freudenberger at about fourteen. Fun fact: his nickname, 'the Raphael of Cats', is often attributed to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, who travelled through Bern in 1807 and admired his work.

title: Cats
collection: Holding institution not identified (watercolour, c. 1800; reproduced on Wikimedia Commons)
description: A tortoiseshell-and-white mother sits upright on a low wooden bench, one forepaw lifted, staring straight out with round amber eyes. Below the bench a ginger kitten grips a bench leg and a calico kitten guards a scrap on the floor. Commons titles the sheet simply 'Cats', a watercolour by Gottfried Mind of about 1800. The bench is drawn in a few quick planks and the shadows fall to the left, so the family seems to sit on a bare studio floor. Watercolour suited Mind: thin, layered strokes build a coat hair by hair, and the bare paper stands in for a pale belly.
context: Les chats, Champfleury's 1869 book, helped revive Mind's reputation among French artists and intellectuals decades after his death in 1814. Mind rarely drew from life: he studied a subject, then reproduced it from memory with strict fidelity. Fun fact: he also spent long hours drawing the bears at Bern's bear pit, and his bear portraits were as highly regarded as his cats. Wikipedia adds that he openly criticised the celebrated cat drawings of Cornelis Visscher and Wenzel Hollar, which is a bold thing to say as a watercolourist from Bern.

title: Portrait of a Court Lady with a Cat
artist_dates: fl. mid-19th century
medium: Oil on canvas in arched gilt frame
collection: Private collection (sold Roseberys, London, catalogue 481, lot 143618)
description: A fluffy white cat sits upright in a Qajar lady's lap, cradled by her right hand, its pink-tinged face turned aside. She rests her head on her other hand, a green jacket open over a full pale-blue skirt, legs crossed at the ankle. At her feet a white swan curls its neck, easy to miss. The painting, about 145 cm high, sits in a pointed-arch gilt frame against a soft blue sky. Look at her face before you look back at the cat: a small diamond-shaped mark between her eyebrows, which the cataloguer reads as a tattoo, a practice once common across the Middle East and North Africa.
context: Qajar painters took up oil on canvas under European influence and favoured heavy paint and dark, saturated colour, with life-size figures and women holding mirrors, fruit or wine as stock themes. This portrait is catalogued simply as Iran, circa 1850, early in the reign of Naser al-Din Shah (1848–96). It is not a museum object: it passed through the UK auction house Roseberys (catalogue 481, lot 143618), and the image on Wikimedia Commons comes from that sale, with a note that it was acquired in Paris on 2 December 2015. Fun fact: the cataloguer compares the lady's forehead mark to a Timurid painting in the Metropolitan Museum, linking a 19th-century fashion to one four centuries older.

title: The Mask: Children and Frightened Cats (La Maschera)
date_display: undated (variant close to The Boogey Man, 1891)
description: A boy in a battered feathered hat leans in from the left wearing a grinning, long-nosed mask, which he holds up to his face with one hand. A grey kitten laps from a bowl of milk in the middle of the floor with a tabby beside it, a ginger-and-white kitten scrambles up the hearth step at the right, and another cat sits at the fireside by the right edge. The real fright lands on the little girl, mouth open, clinging to the older boy who sits laughing with a jug in his hands. Copper kettle, broom and brick get the same care as fur, in a kitchen painted so smoothly the brushwork vanishes.
context: Christie's sold a signed version of La Maschera, dated 1874 and measuring 75.5 × 108 cm, which it called one of the largest and finest variants of one of Chierici's most famous compositions and compared with a work in the Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan. The Reggio Emilia painter was the most important Italian genre painter of his day and the first to find popular success outside Italy, notably in England and Austria. The image attached to this record is a different, unlocated variant, so its measurements and date are uncertain. Fun fact: Christie's credits the near-invisible brushwork to many thin layers of paint and glaze.

title: The Unexpected Guest
description: A silver tabby mother lies on a folded rug in a straw-strewn barn, eyes half shut, while her striped kitten nuzzles in at her chest beside a sleeping white creature with pink ears, plausibly the guest of the title, tucked in as if it always belonged. A red earthenware dish and a blue-and-white plate sit in the straw behind. As in most of Couldery's pictures the animals are small and the fur is worked almost hair by hair. The comedy is in the mother's face, half dozing, half deciding whether to object. No humans required.
context: Plenty of websites give 1893 as the year this painter died, but the death registration says 4 February 1918, at Elizabeth Villa in Sydenham. Horatio Henry Couldery (1832–1918) first showed at the Royal Academy in 1861 with On Dangerous Ground, two tabby kittens finding fish on a table. The largest public group of his work, 42 paintings, is at Glanmore National Historic Site in Belleville, Ontario, from his brother Bertram and sister-in-law Cecilia. This canvas, dated 1874, is known from an artnet record and is in private hands.

title: Persian Cat and Two Dogs (The Standoff)
description: A long-haired white Persian holds the high ground on a flowered cushion, blue eyes fixed on us, while two small dogs, catalogued on Commons as a miniature pinscher and a terrier, hold the carpet below. The pinscher lies in profile, nose pointed away; the shaggy blond terrier sits up and stares straight out like the cat's deputy. A Persian is a gift to a painter of texture, and Dolph sets its soft, broken-edged coat against the pinscher's tight, glossy black hair. The canvas is about 55 × 75 cm (21½ × 29½ in.), generous for a pet picture, and the three share it like sitters in a group portrait.
context: Elected an Associate of the National Academy of Design in 1877 and a full Academician in 1898, Dolph showed there every year from 1864 until 1900, and after studying in Paris in 1880–82 he specialised in cats and dogs. This painting passed through LiveAuctioneers and is privately owned, so the date 1874 given for it rests on a sale listing, and it is hard to square with his move into pet pictures a few years later. He lived in the Sherwood Studio Building on 57th Street, built specifically for artists.

title: Cats by a Fishbowl
description: Three tabbies crouch on a red-draped ledge, chins low, every eye locked on a glass bowl at the far left: the oldest suspense plot in pet painting. The big cat in front flattens into a hunting crouch, a second kitten peers round its shoulder, and a third, wearing a pink ribbon bow, watches from behind like a junior apprentice. Couldery's speciality was fur in tiny strokes, and the bowl hands him the opposite problem, clear water and curved highlights, so the canvas doubles as a contest between two surfaces. Two goldfish drift past, unbothered. The fish have the glass on their side; the cats have time.
context: Lot 249 of Bukowskis' Autumn Classic Sale in Stockholm in 2012 was this canvas, signed 'Horatio H. Couldery', at 45.5 × 61 cm, with an estimate of 50,000–60,000 SEK, and it did not sell. Couldery (1832–1918), a Lewisham-born cabinetmaker turned Royal Academy exhibitor, made his name with cats caught in minor crimes, starting with two tabby kittens discovering fish on a table at the Academy in 1861. John Ruskin, reviewing the 1875 Academy, said of a Couldery cat that it could not rightly be seen without a lens, though the sources do not say it was this picture.

title: Cat and Mouse Jug
description: The jug is the cat: a white cat with brown tabby patches sits upright on a green mossy base, head bowed, and its own striped tail curls round to make the handle. The pouring lip opens out of the top of its head, lined in turquoise. A small grey shape between its front paws is presumably the mouse, which is the sort of joke Victorian dining rooms adored. The body is moulded earthenware dipped in Minton's translucent coloured lead glazes, which pool thicker and darker in the hollows so the modelling reads across a table. Every time it pours, the cat looks down at its catch again.
context: Coloured lead glazes were Minton's trick: the Stoke-on-Trent firm launched its 'majolica' (also sold as 'Palissy ware') after 1848, and Victorian examples were shown at the exhibitions of 1851 and 1862. Naturalistic, jokey designs suited the new middle-class market, and a cat that doubles as a jug fits the formula exactly. This jug is dated 1875 on Wikimedia Commons, where the photograph is a user upload and no collection is named. Fun fact: Victorian 'majolica' borrowed its name from Italian tin-glazed maiolica, which it does not resemble at all, and Mintons made both kinds, keeping the confusion in the family.

title: Dog and Cat: Animal Studies (Chien et chat)
medium: Pen and black ink on paper
collection: Private collection (ex-Galy collection; sold by Le Manuscrit Français)
description: Stalking in from the lower left, a cat holds its head down and its tail hooked straight up like a question mark; a dog sits on the right, head bowed, its head worked up while its body stays a rough outline. The cat gets the more confident, finished line, and the pen moves fast and economically, already recognisably Lautrec's hand. On the back someone else wrote an English exercise about Cromwell, and its ghostly lines show through the browned paper. There are small losses at the upper and lower margins, a tiny stain on the right, and a red monogram stamp (Lugt 1338) in the lower left corner.
context: A schoolboy at the Lycée Fontanes (now Lycée Condorcet) in Paris probably drew this between about 1876 and 1880, if the dealer's c. 1876–1880 is right: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (1864–1901) was in his early teens. It is catalogued as D.447 in M.G. Dortu's catalogue raisonné (1971, as 'Croquis à l'encre') and was cited by Maurice Joyant in 1927. It came from the Galy collection and was sold by the Paris dealer Le Manuscrit Français with a Toulouse-Lautrec Committee certificate dated 12 November 2024. Fun fact: the same unknown hand wrote an English 'thème' on the back of Dortu D.449, so the boy was apparently sketching on a classmate's homework.
_taxonomy_note: Schoolboy sketches c.1876-80 pre-date Post-Impressionism; better a proposed "Nineteenth-Century Drawing, Sketches & Juvenilia" movement.

title: Bowl with Leopard
artist_dates: Unknown
submovement: Persian lustre-painted stonepaste ceramics (Seljuq to early Mongol era)
medium: Stonepaste; luster-painted on opaque white glaze
dimensions: H. 10.5 cm; diam. of rim 22.2 cm
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
image_credit: Gift of Dr. and Mrs. Lewis Balamuth, 1968. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Open Access (CC0).
description: In a white-glazed circle at the bottom of the bowl, a leopard walks left with head turned toward the viewer, drawn in gold-brown lustre and patterned all over with small spots. A small flourish floats above its back, and a spiky halo of radiating tips rings the medallion. Around it come bands of scrollwork and a rim inscription in flowing cursive script. The metallic film catches the light, so the animal seems to shift as the bowl turns, and the cursive band carries on around the whole rim without a break.
context: Lustre was the luxury finish of medieval Persian potters: a metallic film fired onto the glaze that glints gold. The Met catalogues this piece as a stonepaste bowl, early 13th century, 10.5 cm high and 22.2 cm across the rim; it weighs 14.9 oz, per the museum record. Cleveland's curators remark that felines were favoured in Persian art, and this bowl puts one in the very centre of the dish.
reason: The Met reads the animal on this lustre bowl as a lion (Leo emblem); lions are outside the catalogue scope.

title: Self-portrait (frontispiece to vol. 2 of Chinpen shinkeibai)
description: Cushion occupied: a black-and-white cat sprawls asleep on the patterned floor cushion at right, a tabby curled against it, while two more cats doze at lower left. Kuniyoshi pictures himself from behind, kneeling by his desk of books, having given up his seat, a domestic joke his readers would have caught at once. His robe, swirling with flames and dragon scales, was his personal emblem, which is how buyers knew this was the artist although the book is signed with a pseudonym. A long pipe (kiseru) lies at lower right. It is a woodblock-printed book page, so the self-portrait came in every copy.
context: The book is Chinpen shinkeibai (枕辺深閏梅), an erotic illustrated book (enpon) written by the fiction writer Hanagasa Bunkyō and illustrated by Kuniyoshi; the self-portrait is the frontispiece of its second volume, and the Commons copy dates it 1839. Because the book was erotic, Kuniyoshi signed with a joke name, Ichimyōkai Hodoyoshi, and let the cat and the clothes identify him. Fun fact: his cat habit is well documented. He is said to have kept anything from a few to more than a dozen cats and to have worked with them tucked inside his kimono; dead cats were buried at the temple Ekō-in, and the household kept memorial tablets and a death register for them.

submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
feline_symbolism: The cat on the cushion works as a signature: it stands in for Kuniyoshi himself, letting readers recognise the artist behind the pseudonym.

title: Cats' Lesson (Neko no keiko)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e, uchiwa-e format); ink and color on paper
description: Kimono-clad cats take a lesson, and the clothes carry the jokes. At right a black-and-white cat in blue robes plucks a shamisen, mouth open mid-song; at left a pupil in a blue-and-white robe leans over a text set on a wooden stand, and behind them an orange-and-white cat squints at a songbook. The teacher's robe is said to be patterned with bells, gold koban coins and pawprints, the pupil's with cat treats. A red lantern hangs above. It is a fan print (uchiwa-e): the pale rounded cut-out at the bottom marks the fan's outline, so it was made to be waved and worn out.
context: 1841 (Tenpō 12) is the date given for this comic print (giga), and it matters: the Tenpō Reforms of 1841–1843 banned prints of actors and beauties and put Kuniyoshi under the magistrates' eye. He answered with workarounds such as giving fish the faces of actors, and anthropomorphic cats belong to the same sly repertoire, though no source read here says this sheet hides particular real people. Fun fact: a cat that sings and plays the shamisen while others study is about the safest joke available in a decade of banned portraits, since nobody could be arrested for resembling a cat.
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)

title: Series of Proverbs (Tatoe-zukushi no uchi), right sheet of a triptych
submovement: Late Edo Ukiyo-e Woodblock Printmaking (Utagawa School)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
description: Four cats on one grey sheet. Top left, a calico sits with its back to us, gazing up; top right, a ginger cat folds into a perfect loaf, eyes shut, a red spotted collar round its neck, next to a pair of dried fish. Below, a white-and-black cat stretches with its head ducked under its own body, and a calico at bottom right sits up licking a raised paw. A rice cracker and a wooden ladle lie on the floor. The cartouche at top right gives the series title, Tatoe-zukushi no uchi, and this is the right-hand sheet of a triptych.
context: Tatoe-zukushi no uchi (From a Collection of Proverbs) was published in the 4th month of 1852 by Kagaya Yasubei, late in Kuniyoshi's career; the Kuniyoshi Project's series list sums it up as “Proverbs illustrated by cats”. By then he had been putting cats to work for over a decade, from comic fan prints to the c. 1842 Neko no ateji, in which cats contort themselves into the kana of fish names. Fun fact: Kuniyoshi is said to have had a particular weakness for spotted cats and to have pushed his pupils to draw cats too, which may explain why calicoes keep turning up in his sheets.

title: Cat and Mice (Neko to nezumi), from Shingaku osanae toki (Moral Philosophy Illustrated for Children)
artist: Utagawa Kuniyoshi (Ichiyūsai Kuniyoshi, 歌川国芳)
medium: Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: Private collection, Japan (exhibited at the Osaka Museum of History)
description: A grey-headed cat in a dark patched robe sits cross-legged at lower left, grinning with its fangs out and reaching toward a white mouse in blue robes with a pair of chopsticks. The mouse sips calmly from a cup beside a tray of food and sake. The verse above reads osoroshii mono o nyan to mo omowazaru kokoro kara mi o tsui ni toraruru, rendered on Commons as 'anyone so ignorant as not to fear the danger would lose his life anytime soon.' Read the fourth word again: where the sense needs nan to mo, the poem says nyan.
context: Published around 1842 (Tenpō 13) by Wakasaya Yoichi, the series Shingaku osanae toki is translated by the Kuniyoshi Project as “Moral philosophy illustrated for children” and listed among his comic prints. The impression shown belongs to a private collection and was lent to an exhibition of cats in ukiyo-e at the Osaka Museum of History. Fun fact: the cat gets into the grammar. Swapping nan to mo (“not at all”) for nyan to mo turns a sober warning about danger into a miaow, so the predator is audible in the very line that warns about it.

feline_symbolism: The cat is the danger the careless mice fail to respect, a predator used as a warning for children.

title: Onoe Kikugorō III (Baijū), Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Sawamura Sōjūrō V in Onoe Kikugorō ichidai banashi
title_original: 尾上菊五郎の鍋島の化猫
artist: Utagawa Kunisada (Toyokuni III, 歌川国貞)
description: Looming across the top of the right and centre sheets, a giant spotted cat head with glowing yellow eyes and a red, fanged mouth floats behind the actors, while ghostly red flames burst from the middle panel. Below it, Kikugorō, the centre figure under his new retirement name Onoe Baijū, plays the cat spirit of the Okazaki story as a wild-haired old woman, crouched in a heap of patterned robes. Ichimura Uzaemon XII and Sawamura Sōjūrō V flank him, swords at the ready. Kunisada, signing as Toyokuni on each sheet, gives the actors their stage likenesses in full nishiki-e colour across three sheets, one stage.
context: The print advertises a real event: the programme Onoe Kikugorō ichidai banashi, staged at the Ichimura theatre in the seventh month of 1847 as Kikugorō III's farewell run of greatest hits. Kunisada (1786–1865), the most prolific actor-print designer of his day, worked these names into the cartouches so buyers could collect the show. His rival Kuniyoshi made his own triptych of the same programme, with Kikugorō as Usugomo and a giant cat-ghost looming in a ruined temple; a copy of that one is in the Worcester Art Museum. Fun fact: the cat-ghost role was already old by 1847. Kikugorō had first made the Okazaki cat famous at the Ichimura theatre in 1835, and the farewell show brought it back one more time.

feline_symbolism: In the Okazaki plays the cat is a bakeneko, an aged cat that has turned into a shape-shifting demon and disguises itself as an old woman.
